The standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government, begs leave to present the following as its second report:
Your committee has had under consideration items Nos. 426, 427 and 428 of the special supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1937, and item No. 286 of the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1936, and approves of said items of the estimates.

Railways and Shipping
Your committee has also considered provision for capital expenditures and debt retirements involving $9,959,000 which is to be provided by way of loan to the Canadian National Railway Company, and is covered by a resolution standing on the order paper of the house in the name of the Minister of Finance, and approves of same.

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 57, to amend the criminal code.
He said: The object of this bill is to direct the attention of the house to one of Canada's most serious scandals, the great loss of life at -level crossings and on highways. I hope hon. members will read the provisions of the bill as set out in the various sections. The first section deals with stopping at level crossings other than tramway crossings or those which are protected. The second section deals with driving while under the influence of alcohol or narcotics, and I propose to substitute the law of England for the present statute. Section 3 deals with racing and cutting in, two of the main causes of deaths on the highways. The bill provides that a person who causes death by culpable negligence shall not drive a car for two years, and there is an additional penalty provided. Under section 4, on the trial of any female person by a jury one-third of the jurors shall be female persons duly qualified on the same basis as male jurors. Then the last clause provides thait on the trial by jury of any person for an accident causing death or injury, in every case where a

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) gave notice of a question as to whether I or the government had knowledge that a contract was about to be entered into with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for a long period of years, leasing the line from Windsor to Windsor Junction which is owned by the Canadian National Railways.
I may say that no such agreement has been entered into. The agreement in question refers to an arrangement permitting the Dominion Atlantic railway to use the tracks of the Canadian National Railways, as well as the terminal facilities, from Windsor Junction to Halifax. That arrangement has been in existence since 1914, but when the Dominion Atlantic railway acquired the property in 1928 the agreement continued without formal sanction. On recommendation of the Canadian National Railways a formal agreement has been entered into covering the old arrangement.
On the orders of the day:

I should like to direct a question to the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) following a number of complaints from the Toronto district with regard to what are called in this house shark loan companies. I understand that they are sending through the mails a large amount of literature, and that they charge fabulous rates of interest. I found some of this literature in the mail the other day, but it had no post office stamp on it, and I have been wondering how it gets in the mail in the residential districts, particularly in the poorer districts of Toronto. In view of the large number of complaints that have been made about the methods used by these companies I would ask the Postmaster General to look into the matter and see if the regulations of the Post Office Department are being complied with.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intimation that my hon. friend was going to ask this question or I would have had the matter looked into, but I shall be very glad to make inquiries. The matter had not come to my notice previously.

Projects already undertaken-amount required to provide for agricultural settlement and resettlement, $500,000.

This is a very concise
form of legislation, but due to the questions that were asked yesterday the committee was enlightened on its purpose. Some people attach much importance to jobs. I understand that a great many of our fellow citizens are inclined to lean on the government since the leader of the last government told the country: Let everybody come unto me and I will serve them. This time I intend to discuss the matter not subjectively but purely objectively, by way of showing the importance of legislation to every man, woman and child in Canada. Let us suppose for a moment that there is a certain definite number of jobs available, 25,000, or even 100,000; it will not satisfy the country at large. But when a piece of legislation is enacted by parliament it affeots everyone from coast to coast; therefore legislation should be drafted with the

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
utmost care. It is not a matter of pleasing or displeasing anyone; the thing must be discussed without fear or favour. It is either right and good, or wrong and bad, and one has to decide whether it is right and good or wrong and bad.
Sir, this piece of legislation is a consequence of the policy put into force in 1932, as the minister stated yesterday. I wonder whether according to section 7 of the act respecting the establishment of a national employment commission the commission will in fact and in law be empowered to check the expenditures made by the provinces. There is a strange doctrine which has many supporters in this house and in the senate

I have heard it supported by prominent legal minds in this house-that even if under the constitution the federal power or the provincial power have no authority on a certain matter, if there is common agreement they can proceed. Let me illustrate this. Under the British North America Act exclusive powers are conferred upon the provinces on the one hand and the dominion government on the other. "Exclusive"-the word is clear and definite. Therefore suppose that in one instance the provinces have jurisdiction; if that jurisdiction is exclusive it means that on that matter the dominion government has no jurisdiction at all. On the other hand where the dominion government has exclusive jurisdiction the provinces have no jurisdiction at all Therefore if the dominion government is endowed with jurisdiction in a certain matter the provinces have none, and if the provinces have jurisdiction the dominion government has none. How then can we say that the party which has no jurisdiction can by common agreement be a party to the thing proposed? This argument is not only theoretical; it comes to a practical point, namely, the checking of expenditure. The money will be advanced to the provinces, we were told yesterday. Legislation recently enacted, section 7 of the act which was formerly Bill No. 14, respecting the establishment of a national employment commission, provides:
The commission shall, under the direction of the minister supervise the expenditure of funds voted by parliament for purposes of relief and providing employment, and perform such administrative duties with respect to relief and employment as may be assigned to it from time to time by the governor in council.
Having in mind a logical interpretation of the most important sections of the constitution, those that divide the powers between the federal government and the provinces, do you not think, sir, that the provinces will take advantage of the constitution to refuse to permit inspection of their books by the employment commission? And if the matter is
brought to court it is doubtful whether such a contention on the part of the provinces will be rejected. Therefore on the one hand tthe money will be granted to the provinces, and on the other hand it will be impossible to check the eiipenditure made by those provinces of the dominion's money. This is a very serious objection. I submit it now in order that we may have an explanation from the minister as to how the federal Department of Labour will proceed with regard to the checking of expenditures. One method that could be adopted would be to allot a certain amount to the provinces to meet the expenditures themselves, provided that afterwards they may come to the dominion government for refund, with vouchers; then the federal government would be able to check the whole thing. But if the money is advanced to the provinces they can refuse afterwards to have an audit of their expenditures. May I ask bhe minister what he thinks of the suggestion of making first an allotment to each province according to its population or needs, the province to spend the allotted amount and afterwards come to his department for refund with complete and satisfactory vouchers?

The point made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) relates to the efficacy of supervision over relief expenditures which might be exercised by the dominion government. May I point out to him that section 7 of the act setting up the national employment commission refers specifically to the supervision of the expenditure of funds voted by parliament for purposes of relief and providing employment. Obviously it does not apply to expenditures voted by provincial legislatures for such purposes. Of course at all times we have the power of following through our own expenditures. So far as the expenditures made under specific agreements are concerned, may I say that the whole question of supervision is covered in the agreements, and where for example an expenditure is made ostensibly under the terms of such agreement, and it is afterwards discovered that the agreement has been violated, the auditor general may refuse to pass the account and refunds may be requested from the province in question.
Section 7 of a typical agreement may place the situation clearly before the hon. member. It is as follows:
The province agrees that it will maintain adequate records of all expenditures, supported by proper documents and vouchers, and that such records, documents and vouchers shall be segregated from, although reconciled with the usual records of the province.
The province further undertakes to make all or any of the said records, documents and



Supply'-Labour-Relief Plan
vouchers available to the dominion for audit or examination upon request, and to furnish information in relation thereto.
I agree with the hon. member thait the question of supervision is a very important one, and I assure him that in connection with the negotiation of further agreements with the provinces we shall be glad to keep his suggestion in mind.

Thank you, sir. But the time will soon come when the policy of the previous government will have to be repealed. On October 14 the people of Canada said clearly that they did not desire a continuation of the same policies, that they wanted a change. Everyone regrets the careless drafting of legislation passed in the last five years. Every bit of it should be repealed and replaced by good, Liberal policies. Not one piece of legislation will stand the test of public opinion. It was always a matter of having a peg to fill the hole. During the past five years the policy of the then government was one of expediency, and in many cases when the government had its back to the wall it decided anything. But, sir, it is not "anything" that we need; we need something, and something constructive, something which will bring nearer the dawn of normalcy.
First of all we have to make an inventory of conditions in Canada. We must make a survey of mortgages on farms. Here we are asking that money be voted for the relief of farmers, and I believe the vote would refer to relief in the broad sense of the term. Specifically it is to provide "for agricultural settlement and resettlement." Many farmers have had to leave their land because they were not successful in securing adjustments from the farm loan board. Sometimes there was a difference of $200 or $300, and because on occasions the board refused to lend the farmers two or three hundred dollars more, those farmers had to quit their lands.
The vote under discussion is for $500,000, a large sum, but only a drop in the bucket when we consider the needs of the farmers. It is impossible for the government to pay all the debts of the farmers, because those debts are too great. In order to know what the farmer needs it is essential first of all that the government be made acquainted with the total amount of farm mortgages in each province. We must have that information if we are to find out how money can be lent to farmers, either by governments or by other organizations, to permit their survival. If we are to lend money the amount must be defined according to the needs of the farmers, and that information can be secured only by first having the amount of the mortgages. This information is not available at the present

time. The figures supplied in the last census are incomplete and far from satisfactory. If we are to take into account the best way of reestablishing farmers we must also consider the farm loan policy. Not only that, but there must be a careful consideration of the tariff, because we know the tariff plays an important part in the sale of farm products. Further, the Department of Trade and Commerce should play the game hand in hand with the Department of National Revenue, in order to find new markets for the farmer. Therefore I say that under item 329 the whole policy of several departments with regard to farmers might be considered.
As was stated yesterday, there must be one head or one leader in every field of activity. That is my humble understanding. The Prime Minister should be the leader of all the leaders in the cabinet, by directing the policy which will bring about the desired change. We cannot expect a change of any kind if we continue to follow the policies of the previous administration. We need a drastic change of policy. Moreover, every minister should be careful in the acceptance of advice given to him by some deputy heads. I know one of them who is most dangerous, because he is a crank. I am not now speaking about the Department of Labour but about another department with which all other departments have to deal. When a man tries to make experiments on too large a scale at the expense of the country, it is most dangerous. A check should also be made of the few men who composed the outside brain trust of the last Prime Minister, and those men should be superannuated right away. They were behind the curtains, but there they played their role by giving wrong advice. I hope this government will not accept any more of the advice given by those people, and will see to it that they are made inoffensive. The government cannot be expected to settle the question of unemployment even within five years if the policies of the Tory government are continued. There must be an end to that. Of course, I appreciate the fact that farmers must be helped, but in order to help them and relieve unemployment all the former Tory policies must be repealed and thrown into the wastepaper basket, and new and progressive legislation must be brought forward for the benefit of the farmers and other citizens as well. I am ready to give this a chance, but the policies of the previous government have proved a failure, and how can we expect anything by continuing them? The few men who are responsible for the disaster that has taken place in the settlement of farmers should be made innocuous, and I hope, Mr. APRIL 30, 1936
Supply-Labour-Relief Plar
Chairman, that within a very short time I shall be in a position to receive more information about these fellows.
Can the minister give us some idea as to how this amount of $500,000 will be divided among the provinces?

I sought to make it clear yesterday afternoon that this sum of $500,000 includes $250,000 to which we are committed under existing agreements, and $250,000 which will be required to meet the anticipated demands from provinces with which the dominion government has relief settlement agreements. As to the precise provincial distribution of this amount, my hon. friend will understand that this must depend upon the number of relief settlers in each province. I am not able to give him in dollars and cents at the moment the exact distribution. It depends upon the number who have availed themselves or will avail themselves of the opportunity to take advantage of the relief settlement schemes. I put on record yesterday the numbers who had been assisted in the various provinces.

I wanted to make a suggestion to the minister with reference to the problem of agricultural settlement, and particularly as it refers to the province of Saskatchewan. When the drought was at its worst in Saskatchewan, farmers who had been forced off their farms by reason of indebtedness and climatic conditions volunteered to go into the northern part of the province. I know many of them. A utopian picture was painted for them. They were told they would be able to shoot enough and fish enough to keep themselves in food, they would be able .to get enough fuel from the forest, and all they would need would be a little money for clothing. It was painted as a paradise compared with the country they were leaving. I am not blaming anybody at all. The government was faced with a drastic situation and applied what seemed to them to be the best remedy. But what do we find at the present time? Many of these families are now in the northern part of Saskatchewan where the land is so densely overgrown that it will take a number of years to clear even enough land to feed stock. These people are away from roads, railways and telephone communication. Whole communities of them are on relief, and dependent on some type of government assistance, while in the south, the very country which they left, conditions are improving and that country is coming back, climatically speaking. In the part of the province from which I come you can travel mile after mile and see farm after farm
that has been abandoned, with good buildings, telephone communication, good roads, close to the station; with elevators, and yet you will find whole stretches of country uninhabited. Instead of taking people up into the north to settle them there or continuing to assist the settlers who are now up north, it would seem better to enter into some agreement by which the government could take over for settlement purposes farms which have been taken over by the municipalities for non-payment of taxes. A great many mortgage and loan companies own large tracts of land in Saskatchewan and would be very glad to get rid of some of it for the taxes and indebtedness against it. Many of these settlers could be brought back into what is really a grain growing country. They are grain farmers and are not qualified for settlement in the northern part of the province, where they find themselves in a type of country to which they are not suited and for which they have no inclination. I suggest that some such agreement might be worked out. The time has certainly come for a new orientation on this problem by which much of this desirable land in southern Saskatchewan could be taken over by the government and these settlers brought back into their own community, with some of the comforts of life. They would be back in association with their fellow creatures, and a scheme could be set up under which the families brought back could repay at a very low rate of interest some of the debt against this abandoned country. I submit that for the minister's consideration.

Mr. Chairman, under item 310 assistance can be given to settlers to transfer them from a drought area into a more productive area. Item 329 deals to some extent with the same subject, and there may be some overlapping between the two. When the dollar for dollar bonus legislation was before the house I referred to the fact that the soldier settlement board had been formed in 1919 and supervisors appointed for the purpose of reestablishing and settling soldiers on the land. I think a considerable number of them were settled in the drought area in spite of the fact that the government knew then that these areas were not suitable for settlement. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Crerar) has asked me for my authority, and I should like to quote from a letter which I have received on this subject from the Department of Immigration. It says in part:
The area from townships 27 to 32 was subdivided in 1905 in a very dry season. Of the eighty-four townships fifty per cent was rated as too dry and unproductive; thirty-

seven per cent was rated for grazing, and, given sufficient moisture, about thirty per cent was conceded for farming.
Although thirty per cent was cenceded for farming, a far less proportion than that is really suitable for farming. It is not a question of dry cycles at all, because that district has been dry ever since 1905. A number of farmers have moved out of the district but there is still a large number who desire to be moved out, who are on relief and are unable to make a living there. Would they be eligible under this item to be moved into other districts?

The vote under consideration applies to agricultural settlement and rehabilitation. I have already pointed out that this is a commitment under existing agreements for relief settlement, and the purpose of these relief agreements is to take from municipalities families with previous agricultural experience and place them on the land. Obviously in order to qualify for that opportunity they must previously have been on relief. It is not, properly speaking, a scheme of colonization such as my hon. friend perhaps has in mind. The situation to which he has referred and which has been referred to by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) has been brought to my attention. Unquestionably in the settlement of western Canada there has been at times an unfortunate selection of land. That raises a very large question for consideration. I would point out that a discussion of colonization in its wider aspects does not come strictly within the terms of this vote. I have no desire to curtail the discussion or to withhold information, but I should like to direct the attention of the committee to the fact that this item and those that follow immediately relate to projects already undertaken, in other words, to which we are already committed. We are simply meeting our obligations. Any general discussion on any of these subjects would come more properly under the items which follow immediately under the heading "other projects." As I have said, I have no desire to curtail discussion or to withhold information; I am simply suggesting that it would expedite the progress of these estimates if we passed the items to which we are committed already and then dealt with the items under "other projects," most of these duplicate in some manner or relate to methods of dealing with the relief situation which have been already undertaken and tested by experience.

If the minister could spare the time this summer, I suggest that he

personally look into some of these projects already undertaken.
I intend to.

I have in mind particularly the settlement in the Loon Lake district of Saskatchewan undertaken by the cities of Saskatoon and Moose Jaw. People have been encouraged by the municipalities to settle on land in this district, and a tremendous problem is likely to be created due to the fact that some of this land is believed to be deficient in certain essential chemicals. North of this district other people settled on rather good land, but they went in there believing that they were going to get a railway. Incidentally I may tell the minister that if he goes there he will find that these people expect the federal1 government to build that railway. I suggest that before much more of this kind of settlement is undertaken, it might be well for the minister personally to look into some of these projects. Reference has been made to the use of single men in connection with the railways, and I would suggest that labour of this type could be used in clearing bush from land which would be suitable for settlement. People could then be settled in communities where they could have schools and other facilities, and in that way we would be actually reestablishing these people.

I understand from the
minister that the back to the land movement would not come under this vote.
It would be confined to those who are on relief in the municipalities.
It has nothing to do with the back to the land movement inaugurated four years ago?
Yes, but it is confined to those who are relief recipients.

I believe I have more of this type of settler in my constituency than will be found' in any other section of the country. I agree entirely with what certain aldermen of the city of Ottawa said the other day when they advised the recipients of relief to stay in the city and not go on the land. I do not want the government to enlarge this scheme, although it should look after the people who went back to the land three or four years ago. The present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) told me two years ago that after the $600 given to these people had been expended, it might be found necessary to give further aid. I am glad help has been given to some of these settlers, but I do not want to see any more people coming from the industrial centres of Ontario to settle on the land when we have many sons of farmers,

men who are experienced, who cannot get settled on the land. The government should be very careful before going further with these schemes.
Next session I should like to see this back to the land and settlement question brought before the agriculture committee in order that it may be thoroughly discussed. I believe I have about 600 of these settlers in my constituency, and before and during the last eleotion campaign I visited nearly every one of them. I found them to be splendid men and women, industrious and courageous, but in most cases they had come from the industrial sections of southern Ontario. They were ready and willing to take up their new life, but the odds against them were very heavy and in many cases insurmountable. Many of them have found their way back to their previous homes, some of them even walking back. Many of the women to whom I spoke told me that they were dreaming of the day when they would be back again in Toronto, Ottawa, Windsor or some other urban centre of population, although they were willing to make all necessary sacrifices to succeed.
I do not want to enlarge upon this matter, as I realize the minister is eager to have the item passed. But I do not want the government to bring one more man from the older centres of population into the newer sections until it has been found possible to give the necessary aid to farmers sons, who want to settle >on the land and those under the $600 scheme. These young men are thoroughly experienced and would be following their natural lives. The minister is a student of human nature, and if he looks into this question I know he will realize the impossibility of placing craftsmen from the cities on farms in the newer sections of the country. These men are used to life in the urban centres and the odds against them are too great when they are suddenly transplanted' to newer sections. Perhaps next session the government may find it possible to set up a special committee to consider this question. If we can make things more eomfortabe for the rural population we will be making a long stride towards bringing prosperity and comfort to Canada.

Answering a question
yesterday the minister stated that some eighty to eighty-two per cent of those who had been settled on the land in this manner had remained there. Has the minister any information as to how many settlers left their farms during the same period?

I am quite sure my hon.
friend would not expect me to supply that information without having had some previous notice of his question. I am not sure that we have the information, but if it can be obtained from the bureau of statistics, I shall be glad to get it. I agree that it would be very interesting. I should like to point out-this applies to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) as well as to those of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette)-that the dominion government does not place these families upon the land. In the first place, a choice is made by those who take advantage of this relief settlement scheme. Then the approval of the municipality must be obtained, and, lastly, the actual selection of the land and the administration is carried out by the province which is concerned in the colonization activities. In making a selection both of the land and of the settler the province has the advice of an advisory committee, and, speaking generally, the municipality also has the advantage of that advice. I am far from saying that the condition of those who have been settled under these agreements has always been satisfactory. I can quite understand that in many cases it is far from satisfactory, and I shall be glad indeed to keep in mind the suggestions which have been made both this afternoon and yesterday regarding the importance of continued supervision. I am free to confess that I have not yet had an opportunity to see some of these schemes in active operation, and I think that my time would be spent more profitably there even than in this house. But that opportunity has not yet occurred; I shall take advantage of it as soon as it does occur. In the meanwhile I have had consultations with the general advisory committee, with representatives of the railway colonization departments present,, and we have sought to go into the whole matter as carefully as possible. I assure the committee that before there is any extension of the existing schemes we shall see our way very clearly.

One hesitates to criticize
in this matter the minister, or the department, or even the government, because in these last five or six years we have been thrown into a condition for which the country, both in respect of organization and, if I may say so, psychologically, has been totally unprepared. I have great pleasure in associating myself with the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) in the sentiments he expressed a little while ago. I think that the money now being spent could be used to better advantage in creating a good community life for the people who are already on the land and who,

unless conditions get much worse than they are, are going to stay there. The minister points out that his department is not selecting the people who go on the land, neither has it selected the farms or the districts in which they are settled. I am pleased to hear him say it is intended to look into this matter before the nest session of parliament, because if the dominion government is to give financial assistance in this way it must provide the organization that is necessary to put these people back on the land. It is useless to place people on the land when many of those who have been living there have been compelled to leave because of the conditions under which they had to live. If the minister will try to formulate some organized plan for putting people back on the land and making conditions there fit for human beings to live under, as far as I am concerned he will not only be immune from criticism but will have my assistance as far as it can be given.

I rise not for the purpose of opposing the vote but rather to commend the minister and the government for continuing this scheme. To students of social conditions no subject has been more thought-provoking than the drift of people from the land to the cities. Perhaps that is a factor contributing to the difficulties that are experienced in the larger cities in the matter of relief. There are men in the cities and larger towns who came from the farms, young men who thought that tiheir prospects in life would thereby be improved. They must have found out by this time that they made a mistake; many of them would be glad to return to the farms of their fathers, which they never should have left, and which would have been in much better condition to-day if they had remained there, because many of the older people were left without that loyal interest and cooperation which in past days have contributed to the upkeep and the improvement of the farms. This scheme is for the purpose of assisting those in the cities who are on relief to return and resume a vocation for which they are qualified and which they wish again to take up. There is nothing compulsory about it. An individual decides that he wants to go back to the farm, to return to work that he is familiar with. He is now on relief, a charge upon the city and community in which he lives. Under this scheme, with the approval of the municipality and the province and the dominion, the desire of that individual is promoted and a joint contribution is made which establishes him to a certain extent upon the land and provides for assistance in the future. By this means he is not confronted
[DOT]"Mr. Maclnnis.]
with the payment of rent and the purchase of fuel, vegetables, and supplies, with which he can now provide himself in large measure. It may not be an ideal condition; the scheme may not be a one hundred per cent success, but the fact that between eighty and ninety per cent of those who harve gone back to the land have remained, that the large number referred to by the minister yesterday-I think it is 18,500 individuals and about 3,500 families -are being cared for in this way, indicates in a measure the success of this undertaking. I recall very well how severely this policy was criticized in the house by those who are now on the other side. But after all time is merciless in its vindication or its condemnation, and time has vindicated and justified in large measure the policy of the former minister of labour and the former government in this respect. We ourselves had some doubts about it, but it succeeded beyond our most cherished expectations. I believe that a large number of the people who are on the farms will remain there, that they will be better off there than they were in the cities, and that the cost of relief in this connection will be materially reduced. I am glad the minister is continuing this scheme and making provision for an extension of it. I think he is on the right line, and that the scheme is capable of further development.

The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Stewart) says he still remembers how those who were then in opposition, now supporting the present government never criticized the principles of the back to the land scheme. I happened to be a neighbour of the then minister of labour, and I know he put all his heart into that scheme. I criticized the scheme in 1931, because the minister at that time made the statement in the House of Commons that the back to the land movement had been a success without any expenditures of public money. I rose on the opposition side at that time and said it could never be a success unless both the provincial and the federal government found it possible to spend large sums of money out of the public treasury. That is the only criticism of the scheme I ever offered. When, later on, the so-called S600 movement was inaugurated, I do not recall that there was any criticism from any member of the then House of Commons. But I repeat that I do not believe we can enlarge that scheme at the present time without consolidating the condition of those who are now on the land and assisting farmers' sons and others who are working their holdings to stay on the farm, because you will not get a majority of these fine people to remain in their present oc-

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
cupation if ever the industrial situation rectifies itself; you may be positive of that. I have been told by some of these people that in a year or two they are going to walk back to Toronto if they are unable to get a lift on the way. Apparently many of them are not satisfied with their present occupation; I think that is the case with the majority. I know some good came from that scheme, and to that extent credit must be given the previous government, but the responsibility rests with the present government to maintain those who were placed on the land a few years ago so that at least they will be comfortable, and substantial help should be continued in the majority of these cases.

I do not want to hold up this item because, as the minister said a few moments ago, there are other estimates under which the discussion can be carried on with better effect, but I should like to know what has been the average cost per family that is still on the land. Some of these families must have been on the land for a couple of years now.
For more than that, some of them. Perhaps it might be useful if I made a brief statement as to the financial obligations that have been assumed by the dominion government under this scheme.
No doubt that will cover it. What I was chiefly interested in was the average cost of the scheme so far per family.
It would be $600 for the two years, and then in some cases there have been renewals for a further two years at $100. Does that answer the question of my hon. friend?
Yes, that is it.

Since this item refers particularly to a resettlement scheme, under which it was possible to take people from the cities and put them back on the land, I think this is the time to express our ideas in this connection. Yesterday the minister said there had been no coercion practised, as far as those people were concerned, when they went on the land. Even though that was the case actually, we find that in many cases there was indirect coercion. The minister also said some of the members of these advisory committees were people representing the railways. I have before me a mass of reports, some seventeen in all, written since last January by one of the persons in the province of Quebec who was most active in regard to this back to the land movement. There is one
point that strikes me. We give these people something like $600 when they go on the land. In my own constituency we have had many people come from the eastern part of Canada, particularly from the province of Quebec. They came of their own accord; some of them brought as much as $2,000 with which to begin farming operations in the locations of their choice, but what is the situation today? Even though they had $2,000 instead of $600, the only food they have at times is moose meat in the winter, if they can possibly get it, and if it were possible they would be very glad to get back to the cities. The figures do not show the people returning to the cities simply because when we put them on the land we see to it that they stay there. I believe if we were to give them the same encouragement to come back to the cities we would find that the movement back would be very rapid. We put these people on the land; we want them to produce and become self-supporting to the greatest extent possible. On the other hand we dread the day when they will begin to produce, because then they will add to the so-called surplus of products we have to-day. First we say we have too much grain, and then we shove these people back on the land to produce more. I understand, of course, that the idea is to have these people become self-supporting, but, as has been said so frequently during the discussion of this question, if the people who are experts in farming cannot make a go of it how can you expect industrial workers to do any better?
I should like to ask my hon. friend a question. Does he think it is better for a man to consume without producing or to consume while producing?

This is the point I am coming to: if the government finds it good policy to put people back on the land I have a constructive thought to offer the minister, even though it may not be taken into consideration at present. Perhaps when the remarks of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) are considered further it may be possible to give consideration also to the suggestion I am going to make. In connection with the Ford industries in the United States, it is well known that for quite a time Mr. Ford has been considering what he calls the decentralization of industry. I quote from the Encyclopaedia Britannica:
The industry does not use a single warehouse-everything is in transit. The centre of the industry is at Detroit, Michigan, and at River Rouge, Michigan, on the outskirts of Detroit; but with the method of assembling cars at the point of use, a decentralization of

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
manufacturing is taking place and comparatively small plants are being located out in the country wherever proper water power sites are available. Each of these plants makes only a single part; the thought behind their establishment is to strike a balance between industry and agriculture. None of these plants employs more than five hundred men, and in most eases the men divide their time between agriculture and industry. This is one of the most important developments.
I think it might be worth while looking into that idea. If we desire to take our workers out of the cities I believe it might be done by the decentralization of industry in this way.

I should like to answer the question asked by the Minister of Labour by asking another question. We say the unemployed should produce. Why should we think in terms of agricultural production only? Why not think in terms of the production of automobiles, we will say, which are admittedly much more expensive than they should be?
Mr. ROGERS; I should be very glad to answer that question, though I am not sure that I can do so to the satisfaction of my hon. friend. It so happens that our industrial life has become so highly complicated through division of labour that it is practically impossible for more than a few general craftsmen really to produce the things they consume, but in agriculture it is much easier to do that.
Miss MACPHAIL; Is it?

Most certainly; I do not
think there is any doubt about it. The question I put to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) was this: Does he think it is better for a man to consume without producing than to produce and consume at the same time? I think that was a relevant question, because that is the choice that is presented to the people who come under these relief schemes. It is a test of their moral fibre and, of their courage as well, that they should be willing and anxious to produce as much as possible of what they consume instead of remaining on relief with very few opportunities for work. We all recognize that we are dealing with an entirely abnormal situation, but as between the choices proposed by my hon. friend, at least by implication, I should think there would be very little doubt as to the answer.
Mr. Ma-cINNIS:	The minister asked
whether it was better to consume while producing or to receive our consumptive needs in idleness. I should like to point

out that most of our best people consume without producing, and no one thinks it is in any way derogatory to them. And the more they can consume without producing the higher they are in the social scale.
My point would apply right along the line.

All right; apply it along the line and we will go along the line with you. Why not put people back to simple production with the spinning wheel and hand loom? Why not have them make their own pants and shirts and all that sort of thing? That is just as reasonable as putting them on the land to-day to produce their own food. Let us take a realistic view of the production process as it is in this country. Whether it be industrial production or agricultural production, it is to-day a social process in which industrial workers in the city and agricultural workers in the country take part. To-day the farmer does not produce without machinery, and that machinery is not made on the farm. It is made from materials obtained in the mines and forests, which then go through various processes in the industrial centres and out over the transportation systems to the farmer. Then he begins his production. When he carries on production with machinery of that kind he is not producing his own needs. It was never intended that he should produce his own needs by the use of machinery of that kind. He is producing for those who take part in the building of the machinery; he produces the food and they produce the machines. It is specialization of labour. So that if you take people out of the cities and put them on the farms a first consequence is that you are lessening the market for the farmer's products, which he produces with complex and high power machinery. The farmer cannot sell to his neighbour the things he produces; if he is to sell them at all he must sell to the people in industrial centres, so that you are not improving his position in any way or the position of those you are putting on the farms from the cities. On the contrary you are making the farmer's position worse by lessening his market to that extent. These people can be self-supporting on the land only on a subsistence basis unless they have access to machinery and to markets. The question cannot possibly be solved in this way. If you wish to ameliorate conditions and help towards the cooperative production that the world must come to if humanity is to survive, use this money to promote that, but to use it in the way proposed here is useless; you might as well throw it in the lake.

I have heard a lot of argument like that in reference to matters such as we are discussing, and it appeals to me as being just so much bunk. We have all the doctors we need at the present time and probably more. These people could make a living for themselves off ordinary land, but the doctor cannot make a living off a dead body.

My understanding is that doctors are doing fully as well as farmers. We have a lot of farmers who are not making a living for themselves. What always irritates me about our philanthropists is that they are anxious to put people on the land in order to produce food, but they are very careful that they do not set up a model textile factory or sugar refinery or train them for doctors and lawyers. The impression I want to leave with the committee is that ninety-nine per cent of the settlers established on the land in Manitoba have succeeded in remaining there and are in a much better position to-day than when they were sent there.
