Yes, during the terms of the agreements. As I said a minute ago, the vote of $3,527,125 includes the amount required to meet accounts for work already done-that is one item, and it runs up to March 31. Then, it is also to complete works to which we are already committed under existing agreements.

Would the minister give the committee some information with respect to the trans-Canada highway in British Columbia? First of all, in the past year did he have an agreement with British Columbia and if so what was the nature of that agreement? Secondly, does the vote provide for further expenditures in British Columbia during the present year? I have heard it alleged that in British Columbia we did not get a cent for the trans-Canada highway, having regard to the true meaning of the word, and that all the dominion government did was to provide inlets or outlets to some of its national parks. It is alleged that that work was described as national highway construction. It is stated further that on that part of the national highway on which we wanted money spent, namely the part in the lower and western sections of the province, no money was spent. Is any of this sum in the vote to be spent in the future, and if so for what purpose? If any has been spent in British Columbia, would the minister state roughly the nature of the agreement, if any?
There was no agreement last year with British Columbia covering the construction of the trans-Canada highway
Did you spend any?

I am informed a certain amount of work was done on certain sections of the trans-Canada highway, through relief camps which were operated by the Department of National Defence, and also through work done in the national parks. For instance, work in the section known as Big Bend was undertaken entirely by the federal government

Does "agreement with the
province" indicate that the province was to put up fifty-fifty?
That was the understanding.

And British Columbia made
no such agreement-had not the money to do it, I suppose.

There was no agreement
last year. As to the second question, there is provision in the estimates for works to be undertaken with the provinces, and the dominion government will deal with British Columbia or any other province upon the basis of what is possible under that item.

Supply

Labour-Relief Plan
But not under this item?

That is not covered by
this item at all.

There is one point on which
I should like to be clear. So far as Manitoba is concerned, has there yet to be an agreement made with the province for the completion of any highways in the province that were already started in 1935, or is it a fact that the agreements having been made in 1935 the projects will be continued now as then contemplated and that the appropriation now being made will be for the completion of all these projects?

The agreement with the
provinces, as my hon. friend has himself suggested, cannot continue in existence after the life of the relief act, and that act expired on March 31, but we have put in the estimates an amount sufficient to meet what will be required to complete the works covered by the agreement. We shall negotiate a new agreement with Manitoba, and in the negotiation of that agreement we shall take up the completion of the works already started under the previous agreement. An amount is made available here for that purpose.

Is there any danger of any
moneys under this appropriation being diverted to other projects within the province of Manitoba by way of relief?

That really is a matter
of negotiation between the province and the dominion. I would point out that in the past we have acted on the basis of programs submitted by the provinces themselves.

What is the number of
the item in the estimates covering the amount which the minister says would be for new agreements with the provinces?
Item number 335.
Will the minister be good enough to let us know what progress has been made with the Winnipeg sewage disposal project? It is a matter in which we were all much interested last year.

One of the subjects under this item covers the appropriation required for the Greater Winnipeg sewage disposal scheme. It will be noted that the amount here is $900,000. That means that we are making an appropriation of $800,000 to cover the commitment for the work to be done this year, and $100,000 is the unexpended balance of the amount to which we were 
committed during the past year. We are informed that the work has been proceeding satisfactorily.
Will this complete it?

Yes, it will complete the
work as originally planned and to which the dominion government was committed.

May I take it that
amount of $354,000 odd which is given in the table on page 6 of the report of the dominion commissioner of unemployment relief is the amount that has been expended on the Winnipeg sewage scheme up to March 31 last?

The dominion commitment is $800,000 and dominion disbursements $354,612.16. My hon. friend will understand these were disbursements on the basis of the accounts submitted and there are accounts now on hand for further expenditures.
More than the amount of work indicated by $354,000 has been done?
Yes.

Has a definite understanding been reached with regard to the routing of the trans-Canada highway through northern Ontario? The acting leader of the opposition smiles, but I recall that the minister of labour in the former administration during the 1930 campaign made the definite statement in my section that the routing of the trans^Canada highway would be through the northern section of northern Ontario. I must confess that after five years of waiting we do not yet know how the road will be routed. We 'have tried to get information from Toronto but have never succeeded. Ther answer has always been evasive. If I understand the situation aright it is this: that until the province has decided on the proper routing of the trans-Canada highway within its borders, no money will be contributed out of the federal treasury. We have been told in our section, in the riding of Temiskaming and Cochrane that the routing will be through our section. There is an alternative route. One route is via Sudbury and Fort William, and an alternative route would branch off from North Bay to Haileybury, Cochrane, Hearst, and go away down to Hornepayne. Very little work has been done in my section although we had the promises of the late government and of the then minister of labour in the closing days of the 1930 campaign, and subsequent to that campaign, that the routing would be through the northern

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
section of northern Ontario, but we have been left entirely in the dark as to where the road will be routed. I am going to protest against depriving nearly 300,000 people of direct communication with the trans-Canada highway if the routing is not through northern Ontario. I have no quarrel with tens of millions of dollars being spent in the southern section of northern Ontario, but I do not want to see my fine section of the country in the north left out of the picture by being cut off from the trans-Canada highway. The province of Quebec has been certainly left out in the cold so far as this is concerned, but the onus must rest on that province. The most direct route would have been from Montreal to Mont Laurier, Amos, Cochrane and Hearst and on to Winnipeg, but that is now out of the question because Quebec is going to build its own part of the road. Is the minister in a position to state whether the government of Ontario has decided on the exact routing of the trans-Canada highway so far as northern Ontario is concerned, and if so, where will the road be located?

It has been the practice in the past for a province to make its own designation of the route to be followed by the trans-Canada highway. The dominion government merely exercises a discretion as to approval, which in the past I think has been in the main wholly formal. Ontario has [DOT]designated the route of the trans-Canada highway as from Sault Ste. Marie to White River, and from White River to Schreiber. There have been suggestions of an alternate route, but of course it is not for me to suggest anything as to the feasibility of .alternate routes. I do know that there have been proposals of alternate routes which would serve other sections of northern Ontario, but the provincial government by order in council has made the designation I have indicated.

I thank the minister for the information. Apparently we are out of the picture, although we had the promises of Premier Ferguson and of the Hon. Mr. Gordon and several others of the Conservative faith, and also members of the Liberal faith, as to the routing of the trans-Canada highway through the northern part of northern Ontario.
Page Mr. Heenan.
But I am not losing faith, because I gathered from what the minister said that the alternate route would likely receive some contribution from the federal treasury. Is my understanding correct?
You will find out about 1940.
Frankly I am not in a position to answer that question at the present time.
Would it be within the federal regulations to grant moneys for the alternate route?
We are not bound in any way so far as our contributions for highway construction are concerned, to confine them to the trans-Canada highway.
Is the minister implying that we are going to build two trans-Canada highways in that district?

I assume my hon. friend's question is whether or not assistance from the dominion government might be expected for some alternate route. I pointed out to him that so far as contributions from the dominion government were concerned, we were not limited to the trans-Canada highway. In the past contributions have been made in certain areas solely in connection with the trans-Canada highway, but in other areas contributions have been made in connection with subsidiary highways.
Will this be sufficient to complete the trans-Canada highway?
Oh, by no means.
What portion will still remain to be completed?
The vote before the committee is simply to deal with commitments already undertaken.
What portion of the highway will remain to be completed?

Perhaps I might place
before the committee an extract from a report of the dominion engineers who reviewed the situation. They reported to me some little time ago as to what had been accomplished up to the present time and what still remained to be done. Their report reads:
The trans-Canada highway could be com pleted as a through route by the fall of 1938
The estimated cost to the dominion government on a fifty-fifty basis of completing the Montreal-White River gap in Ontario, and improving the balance of the Ontario trans-Canada route to the standard of construction now being used by that province, would be $8,390,650 plus the unexpended balance of the current fiscal year estimated as $555,250.
The estimated cost to the dominion government of completing the Big Bend gap in British Columbia entirely at dominion expense would be $1,950,000 exclusive of the cost of maintenance during construction.
The entire route through Ontario would be built to a high standard of grades and alignments.

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
The poorest section of the highway would probably be just south of Donald, British Columbia, but this short section (seven miles) will likely be improved by the parks branch this season as a part of the Golden-Revelstoke road.
So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, there has been only a small contribution from the dominion government for this purpose. This is due to the fact that in order to bring the existing highways in that province up to trans-Canada highway standards, it would be necessary to make expropriations on a very large scale.
The government has only to complete the highway in Ontario and British Columbia?
That is to complete existing gaps. It would still be necessary to straighten out the highway and generally bring it up to the contemplated standard of construction.
Then we would have a passable highway from Halifax to Vancouver.
I take it that that is the conclusion reached in the report which I have just quoted.
Does the government propose to pay the cost of completing the Big Bend gap in British Columbia?

I am sorry, but I am not in a position to answer that question at the present time. That would not come under the Department of Labour; it would be constructed wholly under the parks branch of the Department of the Interior.
I was surprised at the question asked by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), who aspires to the leadership of the Conservative party in Ontario.
Who told you that?

I heard that and I say quite sincerely that I hope the hon. member will get it. We do not want the construction of a new road to connect with the trans-Canada highway. The hon. member is familiar with the Ferguson highway which is almost completed from North Bay to Cochrane. There is a continuation westward of that highway from Cochrane to Hearst, a distance of nearly 150 miles, and what we want is a connecting link south from Hearst on the Algoma Central about eighty miles in length to give us access to the other sections of southern and northern Ontario. We do not want the construction of an entirely new trans-Canada highway; but the fulfilment of promises made to our section.
That is why I suggested the hon. member should page Peter Heenan.

The minister stated that very little had been contributed by the dominion government to the province of Quebec to bring the roads of that province up to the standard of the trans-Canada highway and he said that to do this would mean considerable expropriation in order to straighten and widen the existing roads. I hope the minister will consider the special situation of this province. Quebec is an old province, having been settled for more than three hundred years, and the roads were not built in contemplation of motor cars, motor trucks or other motor vehicles. The situation here is not the same as that prevailing in the constituency of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). The district represented by my hon. friend is a wilderness; it is uninhabited, and in order to construct a highway it would not be necessary to make costly expropriations. In Quebec the highway traverses many old villages where the houses are built right up to the edge of the road. I hope the minister will take into consideration this special situation and contribute something to Quebec towards the costly expropriations which will be necessary to complete the Quebec section of the trans-Canada highway.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the fifth item in this vote, which provides $190,541 for direct relief. I direct his attention also to item 337, amount required to provide for monthly grants in aid to the provinces, $26,000,000. Am I right in understanding that item 330 is to meet outstanding commitments?
Accounts.

To meet commitments
made by the former government when it was paying to the provinces a pro rata share of the amounts involved?
That is correct.
Then item 337 would be anticipated payments for the current fiscal year under the fixed monthly payment agreements made by this government with the provinces after it came into power?
My hon. friend has stated it correctly.
I was wondering at the small amount of the first item.

That is to meet accounts which have come in belatedly.

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
Will the federal authorities have any check on the moneys to be spent on the greater Winnipeg sewage disposal scheme?

In our agreement in connection with this sewage disposal project we have arranged for dominion representation to be assisted by a technical adviser, who is an engineer by profession. All accounts are to be approved by the dominion representative, who will have close and continued association with the progress of the work.

I assume that the giving of contracts in connection with this work will be done by the city of Winnipeg and possibly the province. During the Easter recess I was made acquainted with certain information with regard to expenditures on this work which seemed to me to be rather startling. The endeavour of this federal authority is to expend these moneys for the benefit of people who are on relief; that is the idea of the enterprise. While I was in Winnipeg I learned, with regard to the building of the fifteen foot section of this sewer, that the cost of material was $50, the cost of labour was about $62, and the contractors received $570 for the section. To me that seems a ridiculous piece of business. This enterprise was for the purpose of extending relief to families in distress, and those families actually got $62 out of $570. I do not know how true this is; I learned it on pretty fair authority, but it seems to me that an incident of that kind, at a period such as the present, certainly requires investigation.

If my hon. friend will bring this particular case to my attention by letter in a way which will permit us to investigate it, I shall be very glad indeed to look into it further. I agree wholly with him that in respect of all these expenditures for relief works we should see to it that they reduce relief rolls. That is the essence of the scheme, and I am not sure that it is carried out as completely as is possible. We must profit by the experience we have had in past years. It may be that we can insert in our agreements provisions which will require that those working on these contracts shall have been employed through employment bureaux and that a quota of them, at any rate are taken from relief rolls.

I think in the agreement we made with the province, and through the province perhaps with the city, there was a provision that that should be done. That was the object and the only one of our giving assistance in connection with this work.

Just for the information of the minister, and in harmony with what he has said, if he will look at the Public Works Construction Act, 1935, in which provision is made for this item, he will find a section providing definitely for the employment of those in need of relief or on relief and the order in which they shall be taken, first, married men, and so on. It is a most comprehensive provision.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) asked me a question a few moments ago to which I did not reply. I think it is rather important. This item is for $7,045,115, and it comprises six different items. I asked if the item had carried, and I meant all the items. The committee has dealt pretty well with every item there. I think probably we should have an understanding if the committee is ready to pass the whole item.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have no further objection.

Could the minister state whether any agreement has been arrived at between the federal government and the government of Quebec regarding work next summer on the trans-Canada highway? I should also like to know if any arrangement has been reached between Quebec and Ottawa in connection with the expropriations. I wish to make myself very clear. In a new country expropriations do not amount to anything; they form a very small part of the cost of building a highway; whereas in the oldest parts of Quebec, where you have to expropriate property in an old village, or farm land in a district which has been settled for a long time, the land is valuable and the cost of expropriation represents a great part of the cost of building the highway. I hope the minister will take that particular point into consideration and will see his way clear to give special consideration to the case of Quebec. First, I should like to know if an arrangement has been made for work in the coming summer, and also in regard to expropriations.

No arrangements as yet
have been made with the province of Quebec. As a matter of fact the statute under which we would enter into agreement with the provinces ha3 not yet received royal assent, but we propose as soon as possible to enter into negotiations with the various provinces respecting the work to be done jointly during the coming year, and we shall be pleased, of course, to receive representations from the Quebec government as to the particular direc-

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
tion in which they feel that our contributions can be used most satisfactorily for relief purposes.

I wish to say just
another word, in order to suggest a policy which possibly would take all settlers on farms, at any rate those in the wooded areas of Canada, off relief this summer. My suggestion is that the federal government inaugurate a land bonus scheme and also a bonus for ploughing. It Should seem to be only natural for a man who comes from a partly rural community to ask for a bonus for ploughing and a land bonus, but I believe that if the minister will do that he will take at least eighty per cent of the present settlers and farmers of this country off relief. I rementber a few years ago, when the late Hon. J. E. Perron was Minister of Agriculture of Quebec, I asked him in the second year of that policy how much he had spent for land bonusing and land ploughing. He said that he had spent, in round figures, $350,000, and that he thought it was the best investment the province of Quebec ever made. It may astonish the committee to learn that in my own constituency, which has the finest soil in the northern clay belt, nearly eighty per cent of our settlers and farmers are on relief. Direct relief to our settlers has been a curse. They do not want it; they want a certain amount of occupation on their own farms, and work, and I believe that it is within the capacity of the federal government to inaugurate a land bonusing scheme in the wooded areas of this dominion. I have no time to enlarge on this, and it is not my intention to do so. There should also be a bonus on ploughing. If these measures are taken, the eighty per cent of the farmers who are looking for relief at the present time will find fruitful occupation on their present holdings and clearings. I say that sincerely, as one who knows the situation. I have spoken to hundreds, if not thousands of our own settlers, and they have told me that they do not want to have money handed to them without doing work for it. I do not believe in governments inaugurating big public works schemes in rural sections, but an extensive road policy should be established. The farmers have all the work they can accomplish on their own holdings; that is particularly true of those in the wooded sections. I hope the minister will find it possible to give a little study to these suggestions, and if he adopts them I am positive that in a year's time he will be astonished at what will have happened as far as direct relief is concerned among the settlers and farmers of our country, and that will certainly make them more selfreliant.

Could the minister tell
the committee the rate of wages paid to labourers on these various projects?

The works are actually
done, as probably my hon. friend knows, by the provincial governments themselves. Tenders are called for by the provincial governments, and they actually let the contracts, the dominion government, making a contribution for this purpose and also exercising continuous supervision of the work as it progresses. In our agreements with the provinces whereby we make a financial contribution for these relief works we have had inserted clauses providing for the payment of current or pre-* vailing wages and also for the recognition of the eight hour day. I think I might take this typical agreement and quote from it the provisions touching the matter raised by my hon. friend:
All workmen shall be hired through government bureaux wherein the dominion may instal a representative, and a proportion of said workmen to be agreed upon by the parties to this agreement shall be taken from relief lists.
This is the agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the .province of Manitoba of July 10, 1935.
(b)	No person other than residents of Canada shall be employed.
(c)	No resident of Canada shall, with relation to his employment, be discriminated against by reason of bis religious views or political affiliations.
(d)	Political favouritism and political intimidation shall alike be avoided.
(e)	The maximum number of hours of work per day per employee shall be eight.
(f)	The rates of wages paid shall be fair and reasonable and shall be fixed by the municipalities with the concurrence of the province.
(g)	Only goods and materials of Canadian manufacture or production shall be used if available.

I should like to support
the remarks of the hon. member for St. Boniface. I think a thorough investigation should be made in connection with that contractor in greater Winnipeg who is taking money in the worst possible way. To me it is the worst kind of graft that a contractor should take for himself the money of the taxpayers that has been voted by parliament for the relief of the needy.

I have secured the
statutes of 1935 containing the Supplementary Public Works Construction Act, which is chapter 34 of the statutes of that year. Section 2 of that statute, I think, meets the point raised by the hon. member for Fort William. That section reads:
The governor in council may authorize the execution and completion of the several works

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan
and undertakings mentioned in schedule A to this act, and for such purposes may authorize the performance of such acts and the execution of such contracts as may be deemed necessary and expedient: Provided, however, that in the execution of such works, as far as practicable and consistent with reasonable efficiency and economy, first consideration shall be given to the employment of those who if available and competent are most in need in the locality in which the works are to be performed, without any discrimination whatsoever; preference being shown to unemployed ex-service men and unemployed married and single men with dependents; and that the minister of the department responsible for the execution of such works may take such action as he may deem necessary and proper to enforce compliance with the foregoing provisions.
Exactly the same provision has been embodied in Bill No. 19, which was brought down by the minister this session, and if I remember correctly the contract for this work also contained a similar clause, so that where the work is done by contract the contractor is under obligation to follow these specifications.
Mr. HOWDEN;	I am not finding fault
with these works, but this rumour came to me through a former contractor who is now working as an inspector on this job. If his statement to me is true a fifteen foot section of that sewer cost S570, and that amount of money was paid to the contractors. Of that amount $50 went for material and $62 for wages. If that is true it is a queer state of affairs to find during this depression, when we are trying to relieve distressed people by the expenditure of government money.
All I have to say is that we received similar complaints, and almost invariably on investigation we found that they were not well founded. I cannot understand how any such condition could exist.

Might I also suggest to
the minister that in checking up on these fair wage agreements the matter of the charge for bed and board should be looked into. I have in mind a project which I drew to the attention of the minister last December, in connection with which the prevailing rate of wages I thought was too low, namely twenty-five cents an hour, and the charge per day for board seemed quite excessive. I remember that several years ago the provincial government of Saskatchawan tried to work out something in connection with the lumber camps in the north country. When the men came out of those camps the charge for board and bed during the winter, and the deductions for the days when they could not work, left them very little indeed after they paid their railway fares back to their homes.
That is a point which I think the department should watch very carefully.

In connection with the employment of the needy I think that section in the act is splendid, but my experience is that it has not been carried out. I know the returned soldier or the needy man is not always the one who is given consideration, and I am sorry to say that in many cases political expediency seems to be the consideration rather than the need of the individual. I know in some sections very little of the money goes to the men who really need it, so I think there should be some contract between the federal and provincial departments providing that abuses of this kind shall not enter into this work. I know of a great many cases in my own constituency, especially during last fall, where men were given work on these projects simply because they were supporters of a certain party and not because they were particularly in need of the money. I am very much afraid that in many projects of this kind more money goes to those who are not altogether needy but who have expressed their willingness to support a certain party for election purposes, than goes to those who are really in need. This was brought to my attention very forcibly last fall; it was quite a scandal in certain sections of my constituency.
I should think that where so much money is being expended for practically the sole purpose of helping the needy, the federal government should try in some way to curb the provincial government which has control of these expenditures. I should like to ask the minister if it is his intention to try to see that some control is exercised by his department over the expenditure of this money, which should go to the men who need it and not to the friends of some political heeler. In that connection I might say also that it was not always men with families who received this money. Very often it was young boys with no great responsibilities, who were given jobs because their parents had influential friends, or for some other reason. I am not saying this by way of making a charge at all; I am simply stating a fact, and I am sure the minister would be the last to tolerate such a condition if he knew about it. So I think the federal department should try to exercise some control over the provincial departments in order that the money which is intended for the needy people should go to those who deserve it.

I am wholly in agreement with my hon. friend as to the purpose of these expenditures for relief, and I can assure

Sup-ply-Labour-Relief Plan

him that we will do everything possible to see that the objects he stated are carried out. We have sought to effect that purpose in the past by the appointment, in the various provinces, of dominion representatives whose duty it was to see that the terms of the agreements were carried out effectively. I can understand that in the past there might have been some departure from either the letter or the spirit of the agreements, but obviously it is our duty to see that these expenditures are made in such a way as to have the best possible effect in reducing unemployment. After all, that is the object of the expenditures.
' A moment ago my hon. friend from Leeds mentioned the clause that appears in the Supplementary Public Works Construction Act. If I remember correctly that clause was preceded by the phrase "as far as practicable." You always have these qualifications, and obviously there must be some restrictions. But that shows the need of effective supervision of the manner in which contractors, for example, procure their employees.

May I suggest that this might be done through the municipalities. In the small towns they always have a list of their unemployed, and are unprejudiced. Also in the parishes and counties it would be easy to get a list. As the situation is now there seems to be no system of that land, and the money is not going to the people who deserve and need it.
I notice that the vote is divided under headings which are fairly general. I wonder whether one of them is general enough to include the draining of bogs or marshes or savanes.
That would come under "new projects."
Yes, the next item.
Have any projects from British Columbia been suggested under this item?
Not under this item; this deals with projects already undertaken, but certain proposals have been made from a number of the provinces for new projects to be carried on during the coming year.

I am in thorough accord with the suggestions made that moneys voted for relief purposes should be employed as far as practicable for that purpose. I am glad to see that even at this late date such suggestions are coming from different parts of the house. I am confining my remarks entirely to circumstances which came

under my own personal observation. Relief money has been voted for four or five years now, but during 1931, 1932 and 1934 perhaps the last thing that one would surmise was that any relief work was being carried on. Men could not get work on any project unless they had a card from the chairman of the Conservative executive in the district. I protested against this then and I am equally ready to protest against it now. I do not think any discrimination should be made; selection should be on the basis of need only. I know one fairly substantial proprietor of a garage who had three trucks on a relief project, and I know of one man who was too proud to go on relief, and who had to borrow money but he could not have his truck put on the highway because he happened to be a supporter of the Liberal party. I know it is a characteristic of human nature to be virtuous when in opposition, and I welcome the signs of repentance which are now evident in certain parts of this chamber. I hope we have seen the beginning of a better day.
The shoe does not fit at all.
I was not referring to the hon. member.
No, you could not. As a matter of fact I had considerable to do with local politics in New Brunswick-
Never in New Brunswick.

-and I had a lot to do with unemployment when the former Conservative government was in office in Ottawa and there was a Conservative government in New Brunswick. I say that as far as those two governments are concerned the money that was expended was expended for the needy, but unfortunately since that provincial government went out of power on June 27 last, the money has not been expended in that way.

Coming from New Brunswick I may be pardoned if I do not allow those remarks to pass without comment. When the hon. member's friends were in power in New Brunswick the handling of relief money was notorious. I know of one case in which relief road work was carried on in my hon. friend's own constituency-
I could give a dozen.

*-under the Conservative government in New Brunswick and in which twenty-five or thirty men were employed, supposed to be on relief and they came to the work in their own motor cars.

Supply-Labour-Relief Plan

I do not like to discredit the good name of Ontario but I think we could qualify in the same role. One newspaper advertisement said everybody was welcome to the Liberal association meeting and applications would be considered for jobs on a certain highway.

Apart from whatever feelings we may have as to what happened in the past, I take it we are all agreed as to the importance of inserting clauses which will ensure that this money shall go for relief purposes. That is the matter in which we are really interested at present. I do not feel that any useful object would be served by going into what happened in the past.

If I understood the minister correctly he said that the purpose of spending relief money for these projects was to take from the relief rolls those who were employed on such works. Let me suggest to him that this is exactly what has not been done.
I agree with my hon. friend that we have a great deal to do in that direction.

I say that is exactly what has not been done. It is a question in my mind whether the enormous expenditure on the trans-Canada highway is in the best interests of the countiy at the present time, or affords most help to the relief situation. Is it a good policy to transport people who are on relief to an unpopulated part of the country, and not give relief in those parts where it is most urgent? Even if people who are on the relief rolls were given preference with regard to employment, this does not to my mind entirely meet the situation, because a great number of people in counties in central and eastern Ontario, although not exactly on relief, are very much in need of work. I suggest to the minister that as the federal parliament is voting huge sums for the trans-Canada highway and other projects it should have something 'to say as to where and how that money shall be spent. I suggest to him that perhaps at this time a 'better policy with reference to road building would be to build feeders to the trans-Canada highway through eastern and central Ontario. At least one hundred miles of that highway go through the county which I have the honour to represent. Last year work was carried on in that county prior to the election. I do not propose to make reference now to how this work was carried on, but the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe) knows all about the patronage element at that time.

I know nothing
about the hon. member's district.

I want to urge the necessity of the federal government keeping supervision over that part of the money which they contribute to these public works. I say to the minister that we, the government and its supporters, are held equally responsible with the provincial authorities for the efficient and economical carrying on of this work. I must say that, in some instances, it was not well done. There is at the present time in Renfrew county a strip of road which was built just last fall, and part of which has already gone to pieces. I do not know whether the federal authorities had inspectors there last year, whether the contractors carried out the terms of their contract, but I know that at the present time the federal authorities are held equally responsible with the provincial government for the manner in which this work was done.
Relief is a very important problem in the county of Renfrew at present. There is an unfinished part of the trans-Canada highway in that county. I have been urging upon the provincial government for the last three years the necessity for starting that work immediately in order to furnish relief, especially to the town of Arnprior, which with a population of four thousand people has over one thousand on relief. It is hard to get the province to take immediate action. My submission is that when a contribution of fifty per cent is being made to that work it is the duty of the federal authorities to urge that it be started immediately, and that they have equal supervision with the provincial authorities. I would further suggest that through the counties of Hastings, Peterborough and Renfrew feeders be built to the transcontinental hiwhway, and that federal expenditures be made in that connection to afford some relief of the distressful conditions existing in those counties at the present time.

Item agreed to.
Amount required to provide for administration expenses generally, including salaries and travelling expenses, $175,000.

As hon. members are
aware, the unemployment relief branch of the Department of Labour has a temporary status, and in the past provision for administration expenses has been made through the provisions of relief legislation. We are now seeking to make provision in the estimates, and the amount of $175,000 is the sum which we anticipate will be required for this purpose in the coming year. .

Item agreed to.
2330	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Commission
Other projects-amount required to provide for expenses of the national employment commission, including salaries and travelling expenses, $125,000.

The same applies to this
item.

What progress is the minister making in the appointment of the commission which, I am sure we all agree, should be working now? Legislation has been passed and announcement has been made as to the chairman of the commission, and I believe hon. members and the people of Canada generally would be interested in having the minister announce the complete personnel and when it will begin to work. If he is not in a position to make a statement just now, could he say when the commission will je appointed?

I can understand the interest taken by the hon. member in the announcement with respect to the personnel of the national employment commission. As the committee is aware, some progress, I think I may say notable progress, has been made towards completing the personnel. I am not in a position to-day to announce the complete personnel, and I believe there are obvious reasons why, before further announcement is made, the complete personnel should be within our knowledge. I believe, however, that it will shortly be possible to make an announcement respecting the personnel of the national employment commission.

Has anything else been
done by way of drafting a plan or scheme for the commission, or is that to be left to the commission?

That work will be given
immediate consideration by the national employment commission, but I may say that there have been preliminary conferences with Mr. Purvis who, as the committee is aware, has indicated his willingness to accept the chairmanship.
Does	the	$125,000cover employees who will work for the commission, or is it just for salaries of the commission and	additional	travelling	expenses?

It is intended to cover all expenditures	connected	with	the	nationalemployment	commission, with	such	fees or
travelling expenses as may be required by the members of the commission, and to cover such administrative staff as may be necessary.

This is about
the only new feature in addition to what was done by the former government. While the personnel of the commission has not been named, I believe the Prime Minister announced that Mr. Purvis of Montreal would be the head of it.
As chairman designate, shall I say?

Chairman designate, the minister says. It would not cost him anything, so long as he is just chairman designate. I believe at this time the committee should be advised as to how much salary these men are to be paid. We are asked to vote $125,000, to include salaries and travelling expenses. If Mr. Purvis were going to ask for a salary, I should not think he would ask for a small one. He is not one of the unemployed, but has been very busy. He is one of the largest industrialists from St. James street, Montreal.
Maybe he does not need the money.

As the hon. member has said, perhaps he does not need the money. So that if it is an honorarium we would be glad to express our gratitude to Mr. Purvis for his effort, and if it is a salary we may expect it will be a substantial one.

As the hon. member will understand, the actual appointment of the national employment commission has not been made. I believe it was fully understood by hon. members that Mr. Purvis had indicated his willingness to accept the position. May I say, however, in answer to remarks by the hon. member which, I believe, were received with approval by some other hon. members, that from all I know about Mr. Purvis, from all I learned through conversations with him, the house and country at large will have reason to be grateful for his offer to assume this most difficult and responsible post. I believe I may also say that when we understand the conditions under which he has accepted the chairmanship of the national employment commission we shall have reason for further confidence in the high sense of public duty held by some industrial and commercial leaders in Canada.

Of course that is true, and we would not expect the government to select as the head of a commission a man who had not those peculiarly fine qualities. I have no doubt that even the announcement of the appointment of Mr. Purvis enlists a substantial amount of con-

Supply-Labour-Employment Commission
fidenee. Undoubtedly he has been a successful man and one whose integrity is above reproach. However I think that is all the more reason why we should know what his salary will be, and what those of the other commissioners will be. If we are expected to pass a vote of $125,000 we should have information enumerating salaries, travelling expenses and so on. If Mr. Purvis is head of the commission, or is chairman designate as we were told, no doubt he has considered working for either no pay or small pay, or a rate of pay commensurate with his merits.
I have no desire to withhold information from the committee, but I can only say that I am unable at present to give the information. I believe my reasons will be obvious to hon. members.
Does the vote of $125,000 cover the salaries of the commission and secretaries?
Yes, it covers all expenditures which we anticipate.
That is, the expenditures of the several commissioners.
Yes.
For how long?
During the coming year.
That would be at the rate of approximately $18,000 per commissioner?
This covers such administrative posts, secretarial and otherwise, as may be set up.
Office expenses?
Yes; it is designed to cover all the expenses connected with the administration of the national employment commission and their various investigations.
And office equipment? Will there be motor cars for the commissioners?

I should say that $125,000 is a large amount of money. It is equal to the salaries for a period of four years of three ministers who, owing to the merging of departments, will not be appointed. That is, the national employment commission will receive in one year the salaries that three ministers would receive during four years, so that the merging of departments will really mean no economy in the end. I would like to make a suggestion to the minister. A member of this House of Commons has done part of the work which is to be assigned to the national employment commission. He is
still ready to do that work for nothing, and if the government is ready to accept him it will save $125,000 because he will do the job for nothing provided he can pick up a staff of people to assist him in the work. It seems a fair offer, to save the country $125,000.
We do not know the names of the gentlemen who will be appointed with Mr. Purvis, but I know that one who will be recommended is a man who has been idle since July of last year. Although he has been receiving a salary at the rate of $8,000 a year he has done nothing except draw his cheque. He has done nothing all his life, and yet he is going to teach the unemployed how to work. I find it inconceivable that there should be in the department a person who has done absolutely nothing all his life except submit reports to the government once a year. He is well known; I shall not identify him more closely than that. Since July last he has been receiving a very large salary. He is still doing nothing and he is being recommended to teach the unemployed how to work. Everybody knows him. It is no secret. I find this most extraordinary, and I hope that the minister will take into consideration the suggestion I have made when the names of the commissioners come formally before the government.

Is there anywhere else, either in the main or in these special supplementary estimates, provision made for the administration of the Employment and Social Insurance Act which has been referred to the supreme court?
The administration of that act does not come under the Department of Labour.
I beg pardon; I thought it did.
In any event there would be no provision for that here. The place would be in the general estimates.

I was just wondering
whether there was such provision made.
The minister in reply to a question in regard to the salaries of the national employment commissioners referred to four commissioners.
Not to my knowledge. I must have been misunderstood.

Do I understand then
that seven commissioners will be appointed?

The act provides that not more than seven will be appointed.
2332	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Commission

Has the government
come to any decision as to the number that will be appointed?
The decision of the government will be apparent when the announcement is made respecting the personnel of the commission.

I am quite aware of that because you cannot very well keep it under cover, but I would like a little information now, particularly in view of the fact that this government, when in opposition, was very loud in condemning the former government, which action I did not mind at the time, for its blank cheques. This, in my opinion, is another species of blank cheque. If my memory serves me aright the salaries of the various commissions that were established by the former government were mentioned in the act itself, at least in some cases, and the house knew when it was dealing with the bill what the salaries of the commissioners would be. The present government now wants a blank cheque for a certain number of commissioners not exceeding seven, and we are not to be given any information as to their salaries until such time as the appointments are made and the salaries fixed by order in council. I think before we pass this item we ought to know how many commissioners are going to be appointed and then we would have some idea of what their remuneration would be.

I sought to explain to
the committee, when this item was first brought before it for consideration, that this amount was intended to cover not merely the fees or living allowances or expenses of the commission but also such secretarial or other administrative staff as might be established t-o assist the commission in its investigations and in carrying out its duties as laid down in the act. This is only an estimate. We are obliged to work on the basis of an estimate. We are entering a now field which has not hitherto been explored. We believe that this amount will be adequate for the purpose, but in advance of an announcement of the personnel of the commission, which, after all, is the decision of the government and not merely the decision of the Minister of Labour, I am not able to give my hon. friend the information he requires as to the precise fee or living allowance that will be given to each commissioner. This commission differs somewhat from others in that it is a continuing body over a period of a year at least, and possibly longer. So far as royal commissions

which are set up under the Inquiries Act are concerned, there is in it no limitation upon the amount which shall be paid to the commissioners, and in the past there has been a wide variation in the amounts paid to royal commissioners, either in the fees allowed or in their living expenses. So far as other commissions are concerned, my hon. friend has in mind perhaps the tariff board and the railway commission. They are continuing bodies, really a part of the civil service, and it is simpler, therefore, to provide for them by means of the regular estimates.

Item agreed to.
Amount required to provide for farm placement scheme, $1,000,000.
Would the minister explain the difference between this farm placement scheme and the farm settlement and rehabilitation scheme? I notice that $1,000,000 is appropriated for each.

The farm placement scheme
is a plan that has been in operation for some years and has been found on the whole a satisfactory method of affording food and shelter, and ultimately an opportunity for employment, to single homeless men who otherwise would be on relief in our cities. The farm placement scheme was commenced under the provisions of the 1931 Relief Act, at which time the dominion government contributed fifty per cent of the cost. This plan was put into effect by Manitoba and Saskatchewan. In Manitoba a total of $10 per month per placement was paid out, $5 for the worker and $5 for the farmer. In Saskatchewan the provision was $5 to the worker and $10 to the farmer. Under the 1932, 1933, 1934 and 1935 legislation the dominion has paid $5 per month in respect of each placement, this being given to the worker. The dominion has made different contributions to Alberta and it is understood that to some extent the federal contribution of $5 per month has been supplemented by the province. I have before me the number of those who have been placed in this way. I received a very encouraging letter from the Minister of Public Works and Labour of Manitoba, which perhaps I might quote. He said:
I wrote to you some time ago about the results of the Manitoba farm placement plan for single men. You will recall that we received post cards indicating whether the boys were staying or not.
Up to date we have received 2,950 replies, out of which 1,937 are either staying or still negotiating terms.
On the whole I think that is very encouraging.

Supply-Labour-Farm Placement

How much was
spent in this way last year?

In Manitoba the figure is
$28,021.20; in Saskatchewan, $18,951, and in Alberta, 84,383.72. Those are the only provinces that have taken advantage of the farm placement scheme.
When the minister expended only something like $50,000 last year, will he tell us why he puts in an item of $1,000,000 for this particular scheme?
I shall be very glad to deal with that question, which I believe is a natural one.
I think it will be pretty hard to explain.

The reason will be found
in the strong support given to farm placements by hon. members from the western provinces during the previous debate. My hon. friend will doubtless remember the remarks of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). There is another factor to be considered. We have determined, we believe on good grounds, to close the relief camps and it is possible that we shall be obliged to make greater use of this farm placement scheme. We may have to offer greater inducements to the farmers in order to relieve the large centres of population of the single homeless men who otherwise would congregate there during the winter months. Obviously this is only an estimate of what may be required, but we wish to arm ourselves with the means of dealing with this situation should it arise. It may be possible that this scheme will be extended to the other provinces.

I am very much in favour of this plan and I always have been. I have always been sorry that more use has not been made of it. I heartily sympathize with the minister who has given his department a great deal of attention. He is very much interested in these matters, but so far as I have been able to ascertain, he is following the same plan that we followed during the years we were in office. He has stated that this farm placement plan has worked out very well and that he has come to the conclusion to make more use of it if he can. Without introducing any politics into the matter, I think that what the minister has said would indicate that the previous government had done the best it could under difficult circumstances. The minister is inclined to follow along the same lines followed by the previous government. It is true he has said he proposes to close the relief camps and I hope he will succeed in doing so.
With the assistance of the national employment commission.

I shall come to that. I hope he will be able to close the relief camps, but he must not forget that he will have to provide for these men in some other way. There will be unemployed single men to be taken care of and many of them will not want to go to work on farms. If the minister closes the camps he will have to find some substitute for them. I think all this shows that the previous government took care of these single unemployed men in the right way. It has been stated in reports, as well as by the minister, that conditions in these camps were quite good. I should like to refer to the many references made to the so-called blank cheques. Apparently the minister has adopted the same line of reasoning. He wants perhaps $100,000, but he puts in $1,000,000 in order to have enough to spend.
It is not a blank cheque as the amount is stipulated.

Technically it may not be a blank cheque, but I think it is the equivalent of one when the minister puts in an item of $1,000,000 when he may need only $100,000. He finds himself unable to make anything like a close estimate of what the cost is going to be, the very reason why the previous government passed the legislation they did. They were unable to make a close estimate of what would be required and the minister finds himself in exactly the same position. He was unable to make a close estimate of what was required, so he decided to provide for an ample amount in order that he might not be short of funds for this purpose.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Supply-Labour-Farm Placement
I think it can be brought up anywhere, that I am willing to withdraw the six first lines of the first column of page 2214 of Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to my hon. friend, he cannot bring it before this committee. He has to bring it up when the Speaker is in the chair.
Well, I have shown my willingness, anyway. I will not do any more. I think that is enough.
Well, we will see as to that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are still on item 333, which was before the committee when it rose at six o'clock.
Could the minister give us any idea of what plan the government intends to follow with reference to this farm placement scheme? I am very interested in it.

As I think I pointed out this afternoon, the farm placement scheme as now operated has been adopted only in the three prairie provinces. We have placed in the estimates this large amount in the expectation that other provinces will wish to avail themselves of the opportunities afforded under this scheme to place single homeless men on farms during the winter months. There is also this other possibility, that the scheme may be extended beyond the winter months. At the present moment I am not able to give my hon. friend a precise plan. Obviously it is the type of project which ought to be considered very carefully with the provinces, and when we meet the provincial authorities, as we shall do within the next few weeks, we shall discuss this question with them.

What I had in mind in asking the question was whether the federal government had some precise plan in mind. It is true that some sort 'of plan has been operating in the prairie provinces during a winter or two, but during this last year no such scheme has been operating in Saskatchewan.

Oh yes, it has, if my hon. friend will permit me to correct him. It has operated in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. As a matter of fact I have before me the figures for Saskatchewan during the last year. Under the 1935 act 6,700 single homeless men were placed on farms in that province.
[The Chairman.]
Was that under the old scheme whereby the farmer received $5 and the man received $5?
That is under the scheme which has been in operation during the last two years, under which the dominion government has paid S5 a month to each man who has been so placed.
But nothing to the farmer?
Not to the farmer.

That scheme must have been discontinued, because I have received a number of communications from farmers who have applied to get under the scheme and who were told that it had been discontinued. Apparently the $5 to the man is being continued but the $5 to the farmer has been discontinued.

I might point out that under the farm placement scheme $5 was paid by the province, and the province has discontinued paying $5 a month to the farmer. The dominion government under this scheme in the last two years has continued to pay $5 a month to the man who was placed on the farm.

I think the minister realizes the need under this item for some type of scheme. I do not intend to go over what was dealt with again and again in the house while the question of unemployment was being discussed, namely the need for some means of providing work for the large number of unemployed farm labourers. Just before recess the question of the blank cheque was under discussion. The minister said that it was not a blank cheque because the amount of money was specified. It seems to me that in a cheque you fill in not only the amount of money but the payee. Yet here is a million dollars to be spent, with no concise or precise details or even information of a general nature as to how the money is to be spent. I think the committee is entitled to some outline of the procedure the government intends to follow in the placement of agricultural labour.

I am sure my hon. friend does not suggest that we should include in this item the names of those who will receive this $5 a month from the dominion government. Obviously that would not be a reasonable suggestion. In ordinary estimates, although an accurate description is given of the project for which the money is to be appropriated, that is as far as one can go with respect to appropriations. In this particular matter we have set forth in the estimates a certain sum for farm placement. That leaves us some latitude to discuss with the provinces the

Supply-Labour-Farm Placement
precise terms under which we shall proceed in this farm placement scheme. The acting leader of the opposition, the right hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), referred before six o'clock to the fact that we were continuing a number of schemes which had been inaugurated by the preceding administration. I make no apology for that. We shall cleave to that which is good and reject that which we find evil; as far as I am concerned I should like to have it understood distinctly, in regard to this whole question of unemployment, that I am prepared to share the credit with anybody as long as we can get on with the job, and that, I take it, is the view of all hon. members on this side of the house.

It will be recalled that the late government appointed an official of the Department of Finance to ascertain whether the moneys which were being advanced for the purpose were being paid to those who were validly entitled to them under the farm placement scheme. Is such an official being continued now in this work, or have his services been dispensed with? That is the first question. The second is: Has the minister seen the report or was a report made by the representative of the Department of Finance with respect to farm placement payments in Saskatchewan? My third question is: How many persons are receiving farm placement payments in Saskatchewan at the present time; of the number, are any of them farmers' sons; and as a result of the investigation by the representative of the Department of Finance, how many of the whole number could be considered as persons entitled to receive the payments?
I have not before me the report from the Department of Finance.
There has been a report, has there?
I am not aware-
That is what I am assuming.

I am not aware of any such report. I know in the past, there was some criticism of this scheme upon the ground that it lent itself to an exchange, so to speak, of farmers' sons whereby this $5 a month could thus be made payable to each of the farmers taking part in that transaction; that is, it could be made payable to them through their sons. I believe that as a result of charges of that kind great care has been exercised in the selection of men to be sent to farms under this scheme. Under any arrangement of this sort I suppose there is an opportunity for fraud. I can only assure the committee that in our discussions with the provinces we shall bring this point to their attention and try to arrange matters in such a way as to eliminate this possibility of fraud as far as that can be done. I say to the committee that on the basis of the information which has been placed before me this would appear to be a promising method of providing relief to single homeless men. I am not suggesting that all single homeless men are willing to come under the scheme, but those who do have some urge to take up a rural life, and our information is that a considerable number of the men remain on the farms on a wage basis during the summer months, during the seeding season and the harvest season, following the completion of the period during which, under the farm placement scheme, they receive $5 a month from the dominion government.

I am afraid that the minister's statement does not go quite far enough. When the scheme was launched by the Minister of Labour of the late government it was intended to meet what was regarded as a situation of some difficulty. All of the single homeless men were not put in camps, and wherever there was an opportunity of providing them with employment on farms it was believed that this might create a sentiment, perhaps not as strong as an urge, but at least a liking for rural life that would ensure their remaining on the farms and ultimately going into agricultural pursuits. It must be remembered that the scheme is not entirely new; it has been going on for a considerable period of time.
Four years.

Yes, four years. Mr. Gordon, the previous Minister of Labour, was satisfied with the results which were being obtained, when information was conveyed to the government that there were abuses under the scheme, and in the public interest it was felt desirable to protect the exchequer from, shall I say, improper payments. Those who read the last report of the commissioner of unemployment relief will realize the difficulties that the auditor general has had and that we have had, too, in consequence of complaints which were received in respect to the broader question. With regard to these farm placements we did send a man to the west; I am trying to think of his name.

Mr. Burgess?

Supply-Labour-Farm Placement

Yes, Mr. Burgess. He was sent to Saskatchewan with instructions to cooperate with the provincial government and see that there was no improper use of the moneys provided for the purposes indicated. My memory is that he is no longer employed; that he was removed from his position. I have this recollection, however, that before we left office there was on the farm placement list a number totalling something like five thousand said to be entitled to these payments, and the check by Mr. Burgess indicated that no such number were legally entitled to receive payment. The matter was being still further investigated when the election took place.
I do not want to be insistent about this matter, in view of the situation, but I am curious to know just how the matter stands now, because at the time the reports were made they indicated that some immediate and drastic action should be taken to prevent the improper use of public moneys under the circumstances to which the minister himself has referred. It was an opportunity for, shall I say, an easy diversion of public funds from one purpose to another. I should like to have that information, as far as it is possible to obtain it, with regard to the period since last October, because during the winter the payments were made more extensively than at other times of the year; in fact it was originally intended to confine the operation of this scheme to the winter. I am not sure whether it was extended beyond the winter this year.
No.

That being so, I think the records of the Department of Finance and of the minister's department will indicate just what has been done since attention has been directed to the situation to which I have referred. How are the payments made now, as a matter of fact? How were the last payments made to those entitled to receive them? Perhaps the minister could tell me that?

In the first place I may say that no report dealing with this matter, sent in by any official, has been placed before me, but I did have some knowledge of certain criticism which had been directed against the scheme in its actual operation. Perhaps I should add also that Mr. Burgess, whose name I mentioned a moment ago as having had some connection with this matter, was sent to Saskatchewan, I think, to deal rather with the distribution of the accountable advance to that province in connection with the drought area.

I think his instructions were to deal generally with all the moneys which were being paid by the dominion, to satisfy the Minister of Finance that the payments reached the persons who, under the agreement made with the Department of Labour, were entitled to receive them. I think that is the fair way to put it.
If any report of that kind is in existence I shall certainly avail myself of it.
I think there is; I was told there was.

As to the payments made to the provinces under the farm placement scheme, we are presented with certificates from the provincial governments as to the number of men placed under this scheme when it is in operation during the winter months, and on the basis of these certificates we make our payments to the provinces. I might give the numbers of men concerned in the various provinces during last winter, because this will indicate that the scheme has had a considerable measure of success. The figures are as follows:
Manitoba	 5,200
Saskatchewan	 6.700
Alberta	 2,269
14,169
In other words during the winter months you have a larger number coming under this farm placement scheme than the average number, let us say, who have been in the relief camps. The scheme does not operate in the summer time.
Would it be possible to know just what money has been paid to the western provinces under this scheme?

My hon. friend will find that information in the report of the commissioner of unemployment relief which was tabled in the house a few days ago, and which I understand has been distributed to members of the house. I trust that it has been so distributed; instructions were given to have that done.
Has the minister at hand the figures for last year?

The total amount is in the neighbourhood of $50,000. Some accounts, of course, have not been received as yet, so the total will be considerably in excess of that figure.

Supply-Labour-Farm Placement

It has been suggested that some abuses may have, and I believe have, prevailed under this scheme. So far as Manitoba is concerned, I was informed by a member of the government that there had been no widespread abuses. I just want to make that statement to the committee, because I have more or less advocated this scheme in the past, though I realize that it is not an entirely satisfactory way of taking care of our single homeless unemployed men. But I would prefer to have them go out among the farmers rather than have them maintained in the relief camps.

The difficulty in connection with this problem is lack of information regarding it by people on the prairies. For example, I have before me a resolution from a farmers' organization, urging that the same bonus be given to the farmers as to the railways, because of the probable effect upon the wages of farm help, which the farmers will be unable under the circumstances to meet. I have under my hand a copy of a letter received by a farm organization in Saskatchewan from Mr. Mitchell, director of labour transfers, in which he makes this statement:
I regret very much that I was not sufficiently clear in my letter to yours of April 16. As you no doubt are aware, the government's policy evolves from day to day, and I endeavoured to intimate to you the position as it was of that date.
That is dated April 24. I can understand that people interested in this problem, receiving a statement of that sort that the government policy evolves from day to day, would not quite know where they stood.

If my hon. friend will
allow me to correct him, he would understand from that letter that the reference to policy related to the finding of alternative employment for men in relief camps.

No, I did not gather
that from the letter. There is no explanation of that sort in it. It goes on to speak of the railways after that.

Well, that has to do with
the same problem.

I think the information
I mentioned should be available to the committee before this item finally passes. I am not going to ask that the item stand over in order to secure that information, but if on some item in the main estimates-I think the minister's main estimates are not all passed, are they?
No.

If he will secure the

I would say that the government is well justified in increasing the vote, if only as a further vindication of the former government's policy in this regard. I suggest that the government would have been well advised to make a much greater increase. From the information given to the committee this afternoon by the minister it was quite evident that those who were assisted on the settlement and resettlement basis secured much less, and that it took much less from the treasury of Canada to reestablish them on the land than it did to pay a man on relief to do nothing. The minister pointed out in answer to a question from this side of the house that he preferred to subsidize men doing something than to subsidize men doing nothing and thereby sacrificing their morale and initiative. At a time like this I believe the government might have been well justified in increasing the grant substantially. They could have worked out, in cooperation with the provinces from coast to coast, different schemes that would have cost the dominion treasury less than the cost of direct relief. The average cost of assistance under this scheme, as the minister pointed out, was considerably less per family -personally I think it would have been more than a hundred dollars less-than the cost of direct relief. I do not think we need any commission to satisfy this house and the country that if we can keep the head of a family working at some remunerative employment and producing for less than it costs us to keep him doing nothing, it is surely sound economics to keep him at work, and it also has the advantage of preserving his morale. But we have established an employment commission and provided this afternoon for their salaries and expenses, $125,000, although the minister told us this afternoon that he did not know how much each of the commissioners would receive, and they are to investigate and find some means of handling this gigantic problem which faces this government as it did its predecessor.
Before the commission reports to parliament at its next session we all hope that the major portion of this crisis will have passed, and it is quite possible that the government trusts that before the commission has found a solution the problem will have solved itself. I think the government, therefore, would be

well advised to consider increasing this grant rather than providing $9,200,000 for new public works to be undertaken in cooperation with the provinces, building public works here and there, thereby constituting a steady drain on the treasury of the dominion. An expenditure of that kind simply means that millions will be spent to employ men in work that is only temporary after all, a few months' work in the summer before the snow comes next winter. It costs more than it would to settle them on the land; there is no permanency about it unless the government is going to ask parliament again next year for more millions for the same purpose, to build harbours here and there and highways in the byways and side roads of this province, and, as one hon. member said, in districts not densely settled the government could easily expropriate land and lay down pavement here, there and everywhere to provide what would be only short term employment after all.
I believe sincerely, and independently of politics altogether, that it is high time the government considered this problem with a view to finality and applied some policy which might have at least some semblance of permanency. The government might well have made provision for a larger vote than is provided here for this purpose. If under this vote you can place the head of a family on a farm, where he can take his wife and children and maintain himself and keep his self-respect in accomplishing something and making his 'own living, it is worth the price to restore the initiative and morale necessary to enable a man to carry on. I think two dollars spent in that way is a much wiser expenditure from a national standpoint than one dollar spent to give a man something for nothing. I think the former government as well as this government probably failed in that respect, and I would urge upon the government, and ask them to urge upon their advisers in this new and highly paid commission which is going to report perhaps after the major difficulties are over, that they should consider during this year an extension of this type of policy rather than expenditures which, after all, amount to only extravagant expedients to meet the needs of the moment and have no permanency about them.

Members who are on the wheat committee are bothered about the wheat situation, and people who have to do with live stock are troubled about the live stock situation. Our problem is not underproduction. We do not need to go out and spend millions to bring in settlers from other countries or to get our own people to go back to the land. Our problem is how to get for our products a price which will enable the farmer to get a living from the commodities he produces. To put more people back on the land is simply to continue going round in a circle. You are on the land; you go broke, and no matter how much you might want to become reestablished on your own farm, it is absolutely impossible. You go broke. Innumerable farmers have high blood pressure and heart disease through worrying, and they have finally had to leave the farm and go on relief. After having forced them on relief, to propose to put them back on the land-why, it is a sort of merry-go-round. You are starting to work at the wrong end. I certainly want to disagree with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe as strongly as I can for I do not think he was speaking as an agriculturist. I do not take up much of the time of the house, but I would like to put myself on record that I sincerely regret this vote is not fifty million instead of one million dollars. I am absolutely convinced that the trouble to-day is that we have an unbalanced population, too many people in the cities and too few people on the land.
Let us try to bring about a better balance.
