Following up what the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Mac-phail) has said, I draw the attention of the minister to something that might possibly be overlooked. We simply cannot overlook the fact which is being forced upon us, that farming as a business does not pay any longer. It was altogether different twenty-five or thirty years ago, but to-day we are faced with a new set of conditions. I should like ' to read an excerpt from a recent book by Stuart Chase. This book Government in Business was published in 1935 and although it deals with the United States, conditions in Canada are similar. I find the following on page 39:
Even in such a prosperous year as 1927, Recent Economic Changes shows a net loss of $1,717,000,000 to farmers as a class, a loss enormously accelerated by the depression. Agriculture has failed as a self-sustaining sector of private business.
While I agree in the main that it is wise to get men out on the land, I think we should be careful not to make our country agriculturally top-heavy. If we do that we will regret it in sackcloth and ashes. We will have an agriculturally bankrupt community for the very reason pointed out by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Maphail). If we can add to this idea of establishing men on the land the idea of establishing in the midst of a little community a factory, something like the sugar factory in the town of Raymond, where I have lived for some time, the farmers will have some means of adding to what they can make on their farms. If a proper combination can be arrived at, we shall be working on a sound basis.
I have lived on a farm all my life. My father was one of the pioneers in Alberta. I know of the good times years ago, and I know what bad times are like. I have brothers who are closely connected with the farming business and I know exactly the problems they are facing. I contend that any industry carried on in farming, such as pork production, dairying of various kinds and other industries, takes the most skilful man and the one who is ready to sacrifice himself, as far as clothing and amusements and that sort of thing are concerned, to make it go at all. If that is so, what is going to happen to the great majority of others? I contend that hon. members would be astounded if they could see a cross-section of the agricultural communities of this conn-

Expenditures of this kind are wise, but unless some other means are provided to enable farmers to make a living, we shall meet with great disappointment.

I had not intended saying anything on this item, but I hear so many arguments pro and con and see so many statements made about agriculture that I thought perhaps I should say a word before this item passes. I have farmed all my life, and I have on a farm to-day a son who is the fourth generation on it. If I had to live my life over again I should go back on a farm. I am surprised to hear hon. members talking about smoke stacks, tariffs and that sort of thing. If we want to build up agriculture in Canada we must build up industry in order to provide markets for our agricultural products. The urban and rural people in this dominion cannot fly at each other's throats; they must either prosper together or go down together. The people in the urban centres provide the markets for the agriculturist. Wherever you find an industrial town or city you will find the farmers prosperous in the surrounding territory. The reason is that they have markets for their products.

I believe that this item is worthy of commendation and perhaps it should be increased. During the last four or five years we paid out about $700,000,000 for relief and what have we for it? We are not one bit further ahead to-day than we were when we started. I contend that the most sensible proposition which has been brought up in this house to deal with the unemployment situation is the proposal to place men back upon the land. Our forefathers came to this country and they settled in the primeval forest. They fought that forest and they conquered. The reason why the farmers are not making a success to-day is because they, like the municipalities, the governments and everybody else, have refused to live within their means. Everything we require, everything we eat and wear, must come from the dark brown earth; it must be taken from the farms and from the land of this dominion. Everyone is familiar with the old story that when Adam was turned out of the garden of Eden he was told that he must till the land and earn his bread in the sweat of his brow. That is what we lack in this country. We have thousands and thousands of acres of land which are fit for agricultural purposes, where men could make a living, but they want the white lights of the city; they do not want to go out and rough it a bit as their fathers had to do.
On several occasions I travelled through northern Ontario and saw there thousands of acres of land off which the pulpwood had been cut, and the people had deserted it. Yet that land was producing, wherever it had been sown, immense crops; they might not mature but they would provide an abundance of feed for stock. I know that any man who is willing to work and has average intelligence could go in there and make a living. I will say further that it takes more intelligence, more hardihood, more of the qualities that go to build up a real man, to make a success of farming than to prosper in any other business in Canada. We shall never be relieved of our unemployment until our people are willing to go on the land and earn their own living. This dole system that we have to-day is breaking down the morale of our people. I am in favour of any scheme that will assist men to go out upon the land and become independent citizens of this country.

What I was about to say is this, that as unemployment has increased during the years some of us have tried to point out that some more fundamental method should be adopted of coping with this great problem. We have been said to be idealists; we have been said to be impractical. Well then, we said: Let the government in power undertake some definite scheme. And I would say that whether the Conservatives or the Liberals have been in power we have supported to the extent of our ability any scheme that seemed to look in the right direction.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?
Certainly.

If my hon. friend were in power, are we to assume that he would follow the policies which were pursued by the Labour party in Great Britain when they were in power some years ago? Is that a reasonable expectation?
Would the minister tell me precisely what he has in mind with regard to those policies? What policies?

I think we are justified in assuming that my hon. friend is in sympathy with the program of the Labour party in Great Britain, and he is continually reproaching us for lack of action in relation to this question of unemployment.
I have not mentioned the Labour party in Great Britain.
What is your proposal?	.
Just a moment, please. If the minister will indicate to me what particular part of the Labour program he has in mind I might give him some idea of the way in which it appeals to me.
In relation to unemployment.

I should like to know what part of the policy in regard to unemployment the minister has in mind. Does he mean the unemployment insurance scheme of Great Britain? If he does, then I say distinctly yes.
That was not what I had in mind.
That was part of their policy.
I assume that my hon. friend must be aware of the policy of the Labour party in Great Britain with relation to unemployment.

That is too general a proposition. I have indicated that one of the most important parts of the policy of the Labour party in Great Britain during the short time they were in office, though not in power, and one of the policies upon which they relied and upon which all governments in England in recent years have relied, was that of unemployment insurance. My friends the Conservatives did attempt to put an unemployment insurance scheme on the statute books. I did not think it was at all adequate. Now it is before the courts and we do not know what will be the outcome.

Will my hon. friend permit me to interrupt once more? He has said in effect that he would support the policy of the Labour party in Great Britain in relation to unemployment generally.

Oh, no, pardon me;
I did not say that. I say that I want to know precisely what that policy is. I refer for the moment to the general scheme that has been adopted in Great Britain for a number of years, unemployment insurance.
If I might complete this now, I would point out that when the Labour party came into office in Great Britain in 1929 the percentage of unemployed among insured work people was 9-6.
What year?
In June, 1929. When the Labour party left office in August, 1931, the percentage had risen to 22 per cent.
That is not a fair comparison; the minister knows it.

No, I do not. I asked for these figures because I wanted to know. My hon. friends are continually reproaching us for lack of action. I would remind them that there is a very material distinction between activity and progress.
You are not showing either.
I am not quite sure what the minister means by activity and progress. I do not think we have had in this country either activity or progress.
We had from 1930 to 1935.

I do not think we get very far by taking certain limited periods during which an administration has been in power in the old country or in this country and trying to draw conclusions, quite disregarding general economic conditions.
If we speak of general policies in the old country, at all periods there they have had as one part of their way of dealing with this problem a system of unemployment insurance. We have urged such a system for this country. The late government did attempt that; the present government apparently are not attempting anything of the kind. A decent sort of unemployment insurance scheme would be far more satisfactory than the present haphazard dole scheme, for it has been practically a dole for many years, a dole on a totally inadequate scale, which condemns people to live below any standard which we should accept for decent Canadians. There is no doubt about that, and if the scheme of the previous Conservative government with

regard to unemployment insurance was not constitutional, there is no real reason why this government should not adopt some scheme that would be constitutional.
There is another scheme that has been adopted to a large extent in Great Britain- since the minister wants to refer to Great Britain-'that is the housing scheme. We have had fantastic schemes of public buildings; I hope the present government will not resort to some of the schemes that the late government resorted to. We seem to be incapable of thinking in any other terms than the recognized channels of public expenditure, huge federal buildings, harbours, wharves, highways. From this corner we have urged again and again housing schemes, but not schemes which are dependent upon the loan companies, and which may to a large extent play into the hands of the loan companies. In any case the poor are not aided by such schemes because they cannot possibly obtain the funds to take advantage of them. We have urged a thoroughgoing housing scheme such as they have in Great Britain. Why cannot the government undertake that kind of thing? In nearly all our cities, as committees of this house have definitely reported, there is a great lack of proper housing accommodation, and we have never had a survey of the housing needs in rural districts, where conditions are even worse than they are in the cities. What is the government doing about that? If we adopted some such scheme as that we might get somewhere.
I hope I am mistaken, but I have been waiting here for three months, and as I see the situation to-day, the government are going on the general principle that if they have slightly lower tariffs, in some way or another foreign markets will open up; foreign trade will increase, and that will solve the problem. To go back to Great Britain, we find that a country which for generations had free trade was forced by economic conditions to abandon that policy and adopt another. Is it likely then that a lower tariff policy is going to solve worldwide problems such as that of unemployment? I cannot think so. It may be that the gov-eminent-I will not say it wants this; I do not for a moment think it does-is banking on some sort of upheaval in Effrope, thinking that if we could keep out of the struggle it might possibly benefit us economically. That might be a way out for Canada for the moment, though of course it would be temporary in character.
But failing some such catastrophe, how can we hope that this vast number of almost one

Supply-Labour-Relief Woikf
and a third million people now on relief are going to be provided for in the near future 7 And not only these people, but as anyone who moves about this country must know, there are tens of thousands of people who to-day are living in the homes of their fathers and mothers or being carried along by their relatives. Everywhere you go across the country you hear stories of that kind; every social worker will tell you the same thing. What is going to be done about this host of people who so far have not come on relief but who one of these days will inevitably be forced to do so? What are we going to do about the young people who are being turned out of our schools and universities? I do not for a moment suggest that the government are not interested in these matters. I 'hope the minister does not think I am accusing him of lack of interest, but I do accuse the government of not bringing forward a well defined plan that gives any indication whatever of being adequate to meet this situation which has so long faced us in this dominion and which is becoming more and more acute.
I say that it is becoming more and more acute, because while it may be all very well to talk of grants to the provinces and for the minister to base his estimates upon what has been given to the provinces in the past, we all know that the provinces are not in as good a position as they were a few years ago. We have the case of Alberta; we know the situation more or less in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and even Manitoba, where many necessary services are being starved in order that their government may by almost desperate means come somewhere near to balancing their budgets. And not only that, but in the past the provinces have been able to devolve a great deal of this relief burden on the municipalities, and we know that the municipalities cannot much longer carry the load. It may be that car loadings show a little increase; it may be that a few more automobiles are being sold this year than other years; it may be that some companies are beginning to pay a little higher dividend; it may be that there is a little upward swing. But I submit that neither in the United States where we see to some extent similar conditions to what we have in Canada, nor in Canada itself is there any indication that within the next few years this upward swing is going to be big enough to lessen in any material degree this problem of unemployment.
For this reason I say that it is the responsibility of any government which is in power
to bring some definite scheme before parliament. This should be not a mere scheme of doles such as we have had, not merely a scheme of public works such as we have had, but some much more comprehensive plan. Some of us have suggested the kind of work that has been undertaken in other countries; a number of speakers referred to measures undertaken in New Zealand, Australia, Sweden and elsewhere, that have shown at least a certain degree of success. Apparently the government has not considered any of these, but has simply fallen back on the old time emergency methods which we have had for a number of years past. When we finally come to this last part of the government's plan we find the whole thing is still hazy and indefinite. I do not know what more we can say. I should hope that my remarks might possibly lead the minister to divulge to this committee to a greater extent than he has. done his own ideas as to what can be done in the next six months. I would urge that he give us some indication of what is to be done in October or November when the men come in from maintenance of way work, and when they are dismissed from the farms. I asked him a few days ago and I again ask him to-night what is to be done with those 5,000 single unemployed men in my own city who are not in camps but who are being fed daily out of the public purse. What is to be done with them? The minister has not indicated in the slightest that he has any plan for dealing with them.
What is to be done with the two or three thousand young people who are unemployed but who for the last few months have received special training in the technical schools of my own city? When the schools are closed these young people will be out on the streets. What is to be done with them? What is true of Winnipeg is true of Vancouver, Montreal, Toronto, and in fact any of our larger cities. What are we to do about this? I do not wish to delay the passing of the estimates; I do not wish to talk simply to be heard or for the sake of talking, not in the slightest. But I would say that the government, having assumed office, must accept responsibility for doing very much more than is indicated in any of the three measures under which they have given to the country their unemployment relief policy.

A few remarks of the
hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. McCann) with regard to the trans-Canada highway leads me to think that I should make some observations. His point was that he felt expenditures of large sums of money on the trans-Canada highway were probably in-

advisable at this time, and that it would be better to deal with the feeders and sideroads running into that highway.
Coming from Sault Ste. Marie I am very much interested in the trans-Canada highway, and so that the minister and the government may have no misunderstanding I rise at this time to speak. The highway westerly from North Bay to the north shore of lake Superior until recently had not been finally designated as the trans-Canada highway. As a result of that situation, during the past several years when fairly large sums of money have been expended on construction of the trans-Canada highway no trans-Canada highway money, with the possible exception of a few dollars spent last winter, was spent on that portion of the road west of North Bay up to the White river terminus coming east from Port Arthur. May I point out that that portion of the road now known as the trans-Canada highway running from North Bay to Sault Ste. Marie, a distance of three hundred miles, runs through a fairly well settled territory and through the three cities of North Bay, Sudbury and Sault Ste. Marie.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that item 330 was carried this afternoon. Of course I am in the hands of the committee. The vote of $3,527,125 for the trans-Canada highway was passed, and in my opinion the remarks of the hon. member are out of order.

May I point out that at that time the hon. member for South Renfrew was dealing with money already allocated and under agreement. I believe the minister suggested that with reference to new expenditures, with which I am now dealing, discussion might more properly be had on a vote having to do with other projects such as we are now discussing.
That is right.

I shall be brief. I wish only to point out some facts so that the minister and government may not be under a misapprehension. In substance I agree with what the hon. member for South Renfrew said as to the inadvisability of spending large sums of money along the north shore of lake Superior at the present time. May I point out, however, that there are older portions of the highway on which that money could be expended, portions which pass through several constituencies where relief work is needed as urgently as in other sections of the dominion. I hope the government will not be steered off its course by the use of the term "trans-Canada highway." May I in passing observe

that that section of the road from North Bay to Sault Ste. Marie will be a wonderful asset to the older part of not only Ontario but Quebec. Three first-class highways of the United States come to Sault Ste. Marie, tapping a large population to the south, and act as feeders for an extensive tourist traffic into Ontario and easterly into Quebec.
We know that to-day thousands of people will not enter Ontario and travel east into that province and also into Quebec because of the condition of the trunk road between North Bay and Sault Ste. Marie, a road which to-day is part of the trans-Canada highway. There are people in that section who need work as badly as any other people, and I merely urge the government not to be scared away simply because the road is named the trans-Canada highway. It also runs north of Sault Ste. Marie some sixty or seventy miles to an important mining area.
If I understand the minister correctly, this sum of nearly $10,000,000 is more or less an estimate, and is apparently-
We are restricted definitely to it.

-but an estimate with
regard to the method in which it will be expended. It will have to be divided up under arrangements yet to be arrived at with the provinces, and expenditures will be so governed. I do not consider that explanation is satisfactory, in view of the fact that for nearly four weeks we have been waiting for these supplementary estimates. Speaking at. the time the employment commission bill was under consideration, the Prime Minister said that a special bill which would give itemized explanations of expenditures to be made would be brought down. It seems to me that the estimate upon which the minister is basing bis views is an expenditure which has been made by the late administration under a policy which was strongly condemned, namely that of the blank cheque. Because of expenditures made by the previous government in the last four or five years the minister is now of opinion that under the arrangement which will be arrived at with the provinces probably about $10,000,000 will be required to carry out undertakings with them. It seems to me reasonable to ask the minister to explain in what way the money will be expended and in what way he anticipates meeting the provincial governments for the purpose of discussing expenditures under this vote.

That is a reasonable request, and when it was put to me before I recognized it as reasonable. I sought to give

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
an answer which would satisfy hon. members. It will be noticed that this amount of money is to be expended in conjunction with another spending authority. In other words, it is impossible for us precisely to indicate the projects upon which it will be spent in any province, until we have reached an agreement with that province respecting joint relief expenditures, to which there would be attached a schedule of works to be constructed. Obviously until this estimate has been passed by the committee we cannot enter into agreements with the provinces. We do not know what amount of money will be available for the purpose.
I might point out, further, that during the past few weeks most of the provincial legislatures have been in session and it would have been difficult, if not impossible, for all the provincial governments to send their ministers of highways or public works to Ottawa in order to arrange such a schedule of works as is contemplated under this item.
Where the expenditures are to be made by the dominion government there is, I think, a careful and scrupulous regard for the established practice with respect to appropriations, but I think it is only fair to point out to the committee that under this vote we are dealing with joint expenditures, and it is impossible to give the details until we have arranged the agreements with the provinces. As a matter of fact, it will be within the memory of the committee that when the relief bill was introduced it contained a clause under which the government proposed to bring these agreements before the house, and we suggested that they should not become binding upon the dominion until they were approved by the house. In other words, we sought so far as it was within our power to bring the entire transaction into the full light of day, which, I think, is a desirable principle of public policy, but it was the view of hon. members not only on the opposite side but in all parts of the house that such a course would impose a grave handicap upon the government in dealing with this situation, and at the instance of members from various quarters of the house that particular clause was deleted.
My hon. friend has also asked as to the method of allocation among the various provinces. That question was put to me before and I sought to answer it as best I could. Looking back over the expenditures of the past five years I do not find any unvarying principle of distribution of the amount available for unemployment purposes. It is a matter of extreme difficulty to make any distribution upon the basis of need. One might say, for example, that fiscal need
brings into your problem the necessity of examining the income of particular provinces and their taxable capacity, which in itself is a most complicated factor to determine. I know that from my own experience in trying to find some sort of composite index which would measure fiscal need in the various provinces. Therefore we are faced with the necessity of trying to bring about as fair and equitable a distribution of this amount as possible, being responsible at all times for any mistakes we may make in such a distribution.
May I direct attention to this further consideration? There are here, for example, items for agricultural settlement and resettlement. If one province, for instance, whose need with respect to relief is similar to that of another province, wished to adopt some method of land settlement as one way of meeting the situation, obviously that would have to be taken into account when we were apportioning some of this expenditure for works among the provinces, and yet in advance of our meeting with the provinces we are not in a position to know how far they will wish to deal with the situation upon a basis of land settlement, and how far they will wish to deal with it upon a basis of relief works so far as that might be facilitated by dominion contributions.
I hope I have made clear to hon. members that we have not put the item under this heading with any intention of concealing details from the committee. On the contrary we originally contemplated that the agreements with schedules attached would be submitted to the house. We are dealing here with a situation, let me remind the committee, which to my knowledge has not occurred before outside of special legislation, in constructing public works in conjunction with the province. It has been a simple matter to do this during the last few years under blank cheque legislation because you were concerned only with agreements and you were not obliged to make any estimate to the house of the amount to be expended. To the best of my knowledge this is the first case in which the dominion government proposes to enter into agreements of this kind with provinces for public works, outside the special legislation of 1919 by which the dominion contributed for highways and so forth.

I think the hon. gentleman is in error as to that. Under the provisions of the various relief acts that have been passed by this parliament, if he will be good enough to look at the reports of the commissioner of unemployment relief, he will find set out in detail the number of the agree-

ments, the sums paid by the provinces, by the municipalities, and by the dominion, and the sum total paid.
After the expenditure was made.
Yes.
But this is different.
Applying always to the preceding year?	.

The hon. gentleman is entirely right; the report is a report of actual achievements and accomplishments, not a prospectus indicating what might be done. To use the language of a well known mercantile agency, it is a record and not a prospectus. That is quite true and I agree with the minister. What I am indicating is that in former years the minister was able to outline the general undertakings to which it was felt that the federal government might usefully give its assistance. For instance, the hon. member for Algoma West (Mr. Hamilton) raised the question to-night of the trans-Canada highway. As the chairman has said, this item has been passed, but still it arises incidentally and inferentially through the payment in aid given by the federal power to the provinces. This item was discussed in detail this afternoon and I shall not waste the time of the committee in discussing it further It will be recalled that we assisted in the construction of bridges, in the construction of main highways that were part of the trans-Canada and also in the construction of highways across the provinces, but I shall not weary the committee by referring to these in detail. *
As the matter stands now, the minister has submitted to the committee an item amounting to nearly $10,000,000 and he has asked us to give 'him authority to fill in the names of the payees without indicating to parliament who the beneficiaries are to be and how the money is to be spent, except that it is to be spent in aid of undertakings agreed upon by arrangement between the provinces and the dominion. That opens dangerous avenues of escape and approach. The government may say: This is what the provinces want and we have agreed to give them some money. We meet with two difficulties. One arises out of the fact that the matter becomes political. Men in one province who are of one political faith have been denied the right to go to work. Furthermore, they have been told that the work would be apportioned in the ratio of the known voting proclivities of the men in the community. That is a matter of written record.
There is a second difficulty, one of which the minister is so fully aware that I shall not do more than merely mention it-the matter
of accounting. It will be recalled that the government of the day being seized of the seriousness of the situation through representations made by interested parties, passed an order in council directing the auditor general to take complete control of the whole question. I have pointed out in this house time after time-and I do it again to-night -that when the matter was dealt with by the government in 1934, in consequence of what we had learned in 1933, we insisted that before a single dollar of federal money would be paid there should be a certificate by the municipality or the otherwise organized authority that the expenditure was correct; second, that the province should place its certificate upon the expenditure indicating its correctness, and, third, that a pre-audit certificate of at least one, and in some instances two of the officials in the auditor general's department should be upon the document before it went to the comptroller of the treasury. When the comptroller of the treasury issued his cheque he had behind him the certificates of, first, the auditor general's department; second, the province, and, third, the municipality or other organization responsible for the detailed expenditures.
I notice in the report made by the commissioner that we now have succeeded in making certain adjustments. Arrangements have been made to get back substantial sums of money; there is one case, amounting to some 8700,000, which has not been disposed of. In connection with some expenditures the dominion has declined absolutely to pay them because the [DOT] certificates were not forthcoming. We have deducted from one grant overpayments made in another so that the matter could be adjusted. The hon. gentleman will remember that in the report he tabled the other day there appears a reference to what is being done to adjust this difficulty. I do not point out these difficulties in any captious sense of criticism as the minister has adopted in connection with the provinces the course that we adopted, but he has not surrounded it as yet with the safeguards which, in my judgment in the light of our experience, are essential to prevent a recurrence of the conditions to which I have directed attention. The minister may very properly contend that this could not appear in the estimates; he may say that it is proposed to safeguard the position of the government in the agreements to be made, but a substantial sum of money is still claimed by those who are entitled to grants in aid. As the minister knows, we dealt only

with the provinces, but there are provincially created municipalities and organized entities by which the general investigation has shown that repayments should be made. In this regard I think the minister should explain to us just what has been done and is being done to overcome the difficulties to which I refer.

Perhaps at the outset I
ought to refer to the charge which has been repeated several times this evening that we are having to resort to blank cheque legislation. I suppose one is justified in using that phrase "blank cheque legislation'' in a qualified sense. I think, however, that my memory of the Hansard debates of other sessions is correct, and that on several occasions, when relief bills were before the house, speakers then on the opposition side asked the government to insert a sum, any sum, but a definite sum in order to avoid the blank cheque.

Yes, but that was the
bill generally, the aggregate.

Quite so, and I am sure
my right hon. friend will recall the statement of de Tocqueville that unlimited power is a bad and dangerous thing, and from the standpoint of the then opposition it was that lack of any limit whatever upon the spending power of the government which was the chief ground for criticism of the blank oheque legislation. Obviously it is at least doing violence to precision of language to suggest that these are blank cheques. They are definite appropriations for specified objects. My right hon. friend is entitled to complain that the object is not sufficiently specified, but he is not entitled to say that it is a blank cheque.
I say that it is blank as far as the payees are concerned.

So far as the payees are
concerned? Well, certainly in some of these items it is quite beyond our power to indicate who the payees shall be.
So it was with us.

For instance, under relief
settlement, or under any farm placement plan. My right hon. friend also referred to the fact that under the preceding legislation, in the report of the commissioner of unemployment relief there were set out the objects for which money had been expended. He was fair enough to recognize that this procedure was to some extent different from the course he is suggesting we should follow today. I well recall the debate upon the relief

bill. It will be remembered that we had inserted in that bill a clause which provided that we should bring before the house for its approval the agreements with the provinces touching these very expenditures, with a schedule of works attached, and it was my right hon. friend and other hon. members who pointed out the extreme difficulty of that procedure and asked us to delete that clause. I remember that my right hon. friend in times past has quoted a principle of equity that one cannot approbate and reprobate at the same time, and it does seem that if, in the debate on the relief bill, he said it would be better from the standpoint of administration for us to drop this clause, he ought not to raise it to-night as an objection to this particular item. I think he will acknowledge the reasonableness of this contention, that never before has there been a situation in which we have been obliged to set out estimates providing for joint expenditures with the provinces. This is, I think I might acknowledge very frankly, one of the difficulties attached to a transition from blank cheque legislation to parliamentary control of expenditure.
Hear, hear.

I am pleased to hear
the applause with which hon. gentlemen greet my rising, because it seems to me-
A coincidence.

-reasonably apparent that the minister has forgotten that the plea for the deletion of the provision in the statute came from his own side. He seems to forget that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) presented so strong a case that there was no answer, and the Prime Minister said, turning to his, shall I say, discontented supporters at the moment, that the provision should be dropped. I pointed out on the second reading of the bill how impossible it would be in practice to give effect to such a provision. I did so at some length, and I also referred to the matter later, but the speeches made by an opposition no more numerous than this have never been taken as having any effect upon a government that is so contemptuous of such an opposition.
They are very helpful sometimes.
But it must be that when those within their own ranks cry aloud, the government must give some little attention to their contentions.

That is the difference between us.

The blank cheque would not be of use this time, either.

The hon. member for S-keena (Mr. Hanson) suggests that a blank cheque would not be useful at this time. There are at least a hundred members I could name, on the other side, who would find it exceedingly useful at this time in their own constituencies and who would not be unwilling that it be used in those same constituencies.
Those who are behind me do not desire that the blank cheque should be used in their constituencies at all; they have ample appropriations without it.
That never was used in my constituency in the last five years.

So high was the regard of the late government for the exalted moral principles of the hon. gentleman against the use of a blank cheque that they would not think of its being so utilized. It would be such an offence to his sense of decency and morality in public life that no one would think of issuing a blank cheque for any expenditures in that particular section of the country. I am sure he thanks the late government for having thus respected his strong views on the matter. I am glad he realizes the humour of the situation. I am only pointing out that I agree that the minister could not, any more than we could, set out details of contemplated expenditures. But he could, as we did through the minister in the house, as the records will show, indicate in a general way what was intended. For instance, it has been asked whether it is proposed to utilize these moneys for what are called secondary roads or feeders. That question came up and was discussed in the house, and certain answers were given. I do not know whether it is the intention of the government to use any part of the money for the purpose of surfacing the roads with asphalt or concrete, but at any rate those questions were asked. I do not say that at that time the minister was able to do more than answer yes or no, but he did indicate that that would be so. When questions are asked, as they have been here, as to what might be done, possibly the minister might give a little further information as to what he contemplates, because he cannot be without some knowledge of what the provinces are endeavouring to secure from him. I can assure him that the demands will increase with the length of time which elapses before the agreements are made, and the sooner that $9,200,000 is exhausted in agreements the happier will be the face of the minister, because as long as there is a single dollar unappropriated by agreement, so long will there be an effort made to secure it. It may well be that by a limitation being thus placed upon the amount available it will be made easier for those charged with the responsibility for administration, but the sooner the names of the payees are filled in, with the limitation that the minister has suggested as to the amount that may be available, the sooner his troubles in that regard will cease and the happier will be his administration. I am only pointing ouL-and I return to it-that the minister admits that

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
his estimate of what he will require is based upon the average expenditure which has been made without limitation, thereby vindicating the soundness of the discretion exercised by his predecessor and the government of that day. The excellence of that discretion is indicated by the willingness of the minister to take it as the standard of his own expenditure.

At the outset I wish to express disappointment that the minister should have brought forward those labour figures for Great Britain. It was a specious argument, and if the minister recalls his economic history he will realize that the labour figures had nothing whatever to do with the Labour government but that they reflected the deflationary conditions accepted by Great Britain as a result of the recommendations of the federal reserve bank of the United States.
In the constituency of Nanaimo there are at- least two major problems, and I propose to refer to both of them. We have several ghost towns in that constituency, small places that grew up around operating coal mines. Not forty miles away, in Vancouver, we have an infinite number of relief recipients. Would it not be possible for this government to make arrangements with the provincial government to reopen some of those mines, give employment to the one hundred per cent relief recipients in the ghost towns, and turn over the coal to relief recipients in Vancouver? If that is done, and done without encouraging profits to those who insert themselves into all the business of the government, it may be possible to establish the fact that relief recipients can be assisted to help themselves in some sort of cooperative fashion. The coal miners will dig the coal and the householders in another part of the country will receive that coal at the lowest possible figure for which it can be produced.
The other problem is the condition of the water supply of the city of Nanaimo. I want to direct attention to that, because Nanaimo is in a precarious situation at the present time. The water supply is brought to the city through wooden pipes, and that system is now out of date. The pipes have outlived their usefulness and may buret at any time. If they do burst a major catastrophe will strike the whole of Nanaimo. That city is asking for dominion and provincial assistance in rebuilding that water system, and the sum of $200,000, if set aside for the purpose, would provide work for a large number of relief recipients. I respectfully draw this suggestion to the attention of the minister.
Carried.

I do not see why there should be all this anxiety on the part of my Liberal friends to shout "carried" in connection with this item. Are they afraid to have the question of unemployment discussed on the floor of the house? I remember a time not so many years ago when they discussed unemployment for days and days. Then they never tired of discussing it, but all of a sudden there is this great anxiety to hush up discussion under this item and not to allow hon. members to say a word about the question of unemployment. After all, we must bear in mind that the present government have been in complete control now for a period of six months. They have had complete charge of the destinies of this nation; they have had an overwhelming majority in this house, amounting to almost three-quarters of the entire representation. The government can do almost as they wish, so it is up to them to devise ways and means of doing something about this perplexing problem of unemployment. For my Liberal friends to shout "carried" does nothing to help solve this problem. I do not think there is a Liberal member who did not discuss unemployment and the economic situation during the election campaign; I do not think there is a Liberal member who did not say that if his party came into office they would do something to deal with the crisis facing the country, but that is all changed now.
The minister was good enough to remind my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre about the situation in Great Britain between 1929 and 1931, pointing out that in 1929 unemployment amounted to approximately nine per cent, and that by 1931, when the Labour party went out of office, the situation had been aggravated to the extent that unemployment amounted to twenty-two per cent. Do I take that from the minister as an indication of his condemnation of the Labour party in Great Britain during those years?

My hon. friend has asked me a question. First of all, may I say that the figures I gave were percentages of unemployment among the insured work people in Great Britain by months from January 1929, to January, 1936.
January, 1931.

Those were the specific figures I gave, but my statement covered the whole period. Now, as to the question asked by my hon. friend. I gave those figures simply because I wished to bring home to hon. members sitting behind my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre the fact that

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
this problem of unemployment, in the experience of countries with Labour governments, has not been susceptible of immediate and successful solution. In the very nature of things it defies that type of solution; yet my hon. friends are continually asking us for action, never telling us what they mean by action apart from the spending of public money. If I may continue-
Why not? the slogan was, "Vote King and get action."

We will take action, but it will be ordered action. I have no objection whatever to marching forward but I want to know where I am going. I want to know whether my next step is to be on firm ground or in quicksand, and I am not so sure that some hon. members are so anxious as to the direction in which they are going. I think there are two things of vital importance-

Would the minister
care to name the members to whom he refers, who are not anxious?
I said that they apparently are not anxious to find the direction before they move. We all know there are people who are willing to move swiftly without having a clear idea of their objective.
The United States trade agreement is an instance.

It seems to me that there are cases in which in the very nature of things we must see our way carefully before we proceed. In respect to this whole unemployment question may I remind hon. members opposite that we came into office during a fiscal year for which provision had already been made to March 31 as far as public works were concerned. The preceding administration made arrangements with respect to works designed to cover the entire period to March 31. Not only that, but some agreements were made with the provinces in July and September of last summer supplementary to the agreements originally made, and the arrangements with respect to direct relief were designed to continue during the entire year. We held a dominion-provincial conference and as a result we increased the direct grants in aid to the provinces by seventy-five per cent during the winter months. We went into the entire situation as carefully as we could with the provinces, and from that time to this I can assure hon, members that the whole problem has received
our anxious consideration, as it would receive the anxious consideration of members in any part of the house were they in our place to-day.
Exactly.

And I do not feel that
my hon. friends should suggest that because we have not done something spectacular we are not making progress. For my part I have much more faith in orderly progress than in swift and spasmodic action, particularly in regard to a matter fraught with serious danger in terms of human values, and I use that term in the same sense in which my hon. friends use it.
Hear, hear.

It is quite evident that
what the Minister of Labour has just said meets with the approbation of his supporters, that is, that he stands for progress, orderly progress, moving in a certain direction. 1 am reminded of a little story of a wag who once went through a graveyard and saw on a tombstone, "Here lies Matilda-Follow me." And the wag wrote underneath:
To follow you I'm quite content,
But damned if I know which way you went.
That idea of following the minister may be all right, but some of us would like to know in what direction the government are going.
Going forward.

The minister says, "Going
forward." The minister brought into the discussion the Labour party in Great Britain, and perhaps I might for a moment deal with what he said in that connection. The figures certainly did show an increase, from nine to twenty-two per cent I think he said, in about two years. But suppose I took the Liberal party in Canada between 1926 and 1930 as a criterion; the percentage of unemployed in 1926 and an 1930 would show a much greater increase.
No, no.

I wish some of the Liberal members would be patient. It is true that in 1930 the Liberal party could not see any unemployment in this country. Nevertheless it was there. By 1930 he had a serious unemployment situation, and it was on account of that serious situation that we had a change of government.

How much was there?

Supply-Labour-Reliej Works
Sufficient to cause a change of government.
No.
Again in 1935 we still had sufficient unemployment in this country to cause another change of government.
And there will be another change next election.

As the minister talks in terms of politics, perhaps I might remind him and other members of the Liberal party of what we saw throughout this country during the last election: "Vote for King and action."
And they got action.

And "King or chaos." Such were the slogans. I have before me a little card, of which hundreds of thousands were distributed, which says, "Vote Liberal for work with wages, security and progress."
Some 'hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
If that is the amount of enthusiasm which the Liberal party can engender when $9,200,000 is provided to take care of about half a million unemployed in this country-

Oh, no; let me correct my hon. friend. He must be aware that this statement is not correct. There is in these supplementary estimates, roughly $80,000,000 -I think I am understating it-wholly for construction works or for relief purposes. That is not $9,200,000.
No, that is one item in the total amount. But this is for relief work, and parts of these appropriations are unspent parts of last year's estimates.
Not of this.
Is this all new?
But I mean all the $80,000,000. Part of that was voted by parliament last year, I think?
Some small part of it, yes.
A large portion.

I think it is recognized by the government and even by the Minister of Labour that no amount of public works which the government may undertake is in itself a solution of the problem of unemployment. But he accuses some of us of wanting to go along too rapidly and not seeing where we are going.
No, wanting us to go too rapidly.

They could not do such a thing. I would like them to go a little more rapidly than they are going. We have had this vote of $9,000,000 before the committee for about one hour, and some Liberal members think there has been too much talk on the item. I think my hon. friends of the Liberal party might show a little more patience, for those of the group to which I belong do not indulge in these interruptions very often. But, after all, if we differ from the Minister of Labour in our attitude towards this problem it is because we have a different understanding of the situation. I do not for a moment claim that the minister and other members of the Liberal party are individually not sympathetic towards the unemployed, as I am. It is not a question of sympathy; we are sent here because we have these different viewpoints, and this evening I am expressing the viewpoint of those who sent me here. Those whom I represent think the government are not moving quickly enough in dealing with this problem. During the past six months there has been no diminution worth talking about in the number of unemployed in this country, and I venture to assert that when the House of Commons meets again a year hence we shall still be faced with just as great an unemployment problem as exists at the present time, for the simple reason that no amount of money spent in temporary public works is anything more than a mere palliative. We are asking the government to give something more than a palliative for unemployment.
What, in particular?

We have made all kinds of
suggestions, and they have fallen on barren ground. I moved a motion to pension people who had reached sixty years of age, and to take them out of industry. The Liberal party was told by its Minister of Finance to vote the motion down. Of course he said, "Where is the money to come from?" I am asking the same question: Where will this $80,000,000 come from?
That is less than $500,000,000.
My hon. friend knows better than that. He knows he is misleading the committee and misleading his own constituents, as I happen to know.

Order. I would ask that the hon. member be asked to take

that back. He knows he is not within the rules of the house when he states that I know I am misleading the committee.
He did not say you knew.
I do not wish to say anything that might hurt the feelings of the hon. member.
It is not a question of feelings, at all.
I wonder that some of these hon. members so unruly to-night would not be patient.
Order.
I am just-

speechtext: I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North had better withdraw his remarks. I know he wishes to conduct this debate on a high plane, and I think he will do so.

Of course I do not wish to
do anything that transgresses the rules of the house.
Withdraw.
Withdraw.

Oh, can you be quiet a
minute! If I have said anything that transgresses the rules of the house, I certainly withdraw it. At the same time if the hon. member does not know better, he ought to know better than to make the statement he did.

I do not think
that is a proper withdrawal, under the rules of the house.
Of course it is.

The withdrawal
should be made unreservedly by the hon. member, who knows better than to say the things he has just said.

On the point of order
may I say that the hon. member for Melfort has just charged the hon. meimlber for Winnipeg North with knowing better.

Knowing what
the leader of the opposition has neglected to point out, namely that I am charging the hon. member with not being within the rules of the house, and with knowing that he is not within the rules of the house when he does not withdraw the charge unreservedly.
I would not like to hurt the feelings of the hon. member for Melfort.
It is not a case of feelings.

I withdraw the remark unreservedly and unqualifiedly. As regards the $500,000,000 which the hon. member mentioned, may I say that the figure is entirely erroneous, and if at some time the hon. member for Melfort will take a moment's time to go over the figure he will find how absolutely wrong he really is.
$522,000,000 is the correct figure.

I will not argue the matter. The hon. member is beyond me.
I wish to point out the viewpoints held by some hon. members, which differ from those held by hon. members in this corner of the house. May I point out also that when asked for concrete proposals some of us have suggested the pensioning of people at sixty years of age, and a much shorter working day. I know that to some hon. members the proposal for a six hour work day may seem peculiar, and I can see some who hold up their hands in holy horror when they think of people working for only six hours each day. I observe, however, that in the United States people as respectable as the president are advocating a six hour day for men engaged in industry, so that in some way the country would be in a position to absorb the unemployed into useful occupations. Whether or not this government likes it, or whether or not future governments like it, the shorter work day, increased purchasing power and pensioning at sixty years of age will come about, in spite of governments. There is in the ranks of the Liberal party and in the ranks of other parties in this chamber a growing conviction that the pensionable age of seventy will have to be reduced before long. More than one Liberal member has come to me and told me that he would like to support a proposal of that kind. A shorter work day is something which will have to be made effective before very long.
It is true that the government attempted to put on the statute books legislation dealing with the eight hour day, believing that that shorter day would absorb a great many people into industry. Even the eight hour day is obsolete, although many people engaged in certain occupations are compelled to work much longer hours. When hon. members point their fingers at our group and ask us what we are going to do under the circumstances, I say to them that I have enumerated just two or three items in our policy. May I say, further, that although there may be

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
difficulties in bringing about the changes I have suggested, it is also extremely difficult to continue in the same way as we are going at the present time. Because when we have, as at present, approximately one half million people in the ranks of the unemployed, and when we have no hope of their being absorbed into industry, what is the future of the country going to be? What are the youth of Canada going to do, hundreds of thousands of whom have never done a day's work in their lives, many of whom are unable to find useful employment and to become useful citizens? Is there in the program offered by the government up to the present time anything which will bring about more or less of a permanent solution of the unemployment problem? I do not think so.
The government has enunciated three items or three policies in its program for the relief of unemployment. One is the employment commission; the second is the expansion of trade and the third is a relief program. I do not think the first solution, namely the employment commission, will solve the problem of unemployment. In discussing the work of the commission I believe the minister has said that it would be temporary and that it would attempt to liquidate the problem in so far as it affected the provinces. Then, public works are only a temporary remedy; they bring about only a measure of temporary relief. As has been pointed out by the leader of the opposition, the money provided for public works in the present year is no more than was provided in years gone by, yet in those cities or districts where the money was spent only a very small proportion of the men out of work were absorbed.
So far as the next item, namely expansion of trade, is concerned, I am afraid that it is one thing to be in favour of a policy and another thing to cany it out. So, while I would do all within my power to assist a government in providing or finding markets abroad, I must contend that the first people who ought to be supplied with the necessities of life are not those who live in other parts of the world but those living right here in Canada. There is no greater potential market for the goods we produce than the one here at home. Why talk about sending our wheat or other surplus commodities to the people of other nations, when there is such a great demand among our own unemployed for the things we have in Canada which should be made available to them. One of the first actions of the government should be to attempt to bridge the gap between consumption and production, and until a government

attacks the problem of bringing about a reasonable equality between consumption and production, meanwhile maintaining production at a high level, I claim there can be no solution for the problem of unemployment. For until such time as we have reasonable equality, maintaining a high level of production and a high level of consumption, I say that the government is travelling in the wrong direction in its efforts to meet the unemployment problem.
The problem as we have it to-day is by no means a temporary one, and we should not as a parliament attempt to deal with it as such, for it is a problem which has persisted in maintaining itself for a period now of approximately six years, after the methods of relief and public works have been applied and it has not yielded to any form of treatment. The government, I say, should therefore learn from past experience and turn their efforts in a completely different direction. But they are not doing that. If the government were opening new avenues of dealing with the unemployment problem we might look on the measures which they are now adopting with a good deal more sympathy than we do now, even though I do say that it is essential in the circumstances to have these appropriations passed in order to meet the unemployment situation which to-day exists. But the unemployment problem instead of being temporary in nature is, I believe, now a permanent feature of the economic situation as it has now developed in this and other countries. In the United States they have spent billions upon billions of dollars in attempting to deal with the unemployment problem, and it is quite true that the billions and billions of dollars they have pumped into their economic life might have had the effect of giving renewed life to the industries of that country, but in spite of that fact the moment they stopped pumping money into the economic life of the country there was a recession in trade. Even in Canada the increase in the volume of trade that has manifested itself has been due to the amount of public expenditures which the previous government had undertaken.
As I said a moment ago, if the government are anxious to deal with the unemployment problem in a way that is fundamental they have to depart from the old ways of dealing with it and to try something different and apart from public works and apart from relief. They have to get away from the idea that markets are open for the expansion of trade. I am quite sure that the previous govern-

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
ment were just as anxious as the present one, even though they may have adopted an entirely different policy, for an expansion of our trade. Their intention was just as honest and just as sincere as that of the present government. I had hoped that the minister would have adopted something new or at least departed from the old line policy and, as was promised so frequently during the past election, given the people of this country some hope of future economic security. But in all that the government have attempted in the past six months since they have been in office there is nothing very much different from what the previous government attempted.

Does not my hon. friend think in dealing with this question either here or elsewhere it is of some value to profit from experience? He has suggested a departure into some new way. I have no objection to some new way provided I can see where it leads.

One is bound sometimes to undertake experiments and blaze a new trail. If we had always followed the policy which the minister now commends no progress whatever would have been made. It is only by people taking chances, by scientists taking chances, by medical science and every other form of science taking chances, that any progress is made, and the same principle holds in economics. If we are going to make progress we shall be compelled to blaze a new trail and travel in a new direction even in the sphere of economics because the old order has completely failed. It has not found a way out; it has not offered a solution, and what is more it has not given and does not give to-day a ray of hope to the hundreds of thousands of people in this dominion who are out of work.
I know the minister is just as anxious as I am or as any other hon. member is to do something for the unemployed in this country. No one for a moment doubts his motives. I never have doubted for a moment the motives and good intentions of the minister, but I feel that his methods and the methods of the government are entirely inadequate to cope with the serious situation which has developed and which faces us in Canada to-day. Possibly my plea to the minister may not fall at this time on fertile ground. I know that his friends in his own city have a high regard for the Minister of Labour and even they are expecting a great deal of him. I also have a high personal regard for the Minister of Labour, as I think the members of the house in general have,
and I have a great deal of sympathy for him because he has been put into a position in the government where he has the most difficult problem to deal with of any minister bar none. We all realize that, and if to-day we offer criticism it is not criticism of the minister personally; it is criticism of the action of the government for not attempting to blaze a new trail, because in my opinion only by blazing new trails shall we arrive at some measure of solution of this unemployment problem.
The minister dealt with the position of Great Britain from 1929 to 1931. I assume he must be cognizant of what the government of New Zealand is doing at the present time. They have an unemployment situation to face, but have they said: We are going to maintain and follow the trails of the old parties? No, they have decided to blaze a new trail, to travel in an entirely new direction. Do they know where they are going? I assume they do, and even if they do make mistakes I would far rather the government make mistakes in attempting to do something than do very little and make no mistakes at all.

The minister in the course of his observations made a statement that impels me to rise for the purpose of directing the attention of some of the new members of the house to the fact that for five years we sat on the treasury benches and we listened to attacks, not for hours but for days, against measures just such as those which are now being recommended to this committee. The minister suggested that there were some who did not desire to see ordered progress. He was not in the house in those days, but he must recall the dark days of 1932 and 1933, when we were confronted with conditions which this country had to face, and did we have a word of sympathy, a word of appreciation, a word of understanding? Not one word of helpful criticism or constructive assistance. We were attacked not only for hours but for days and days and days, just because we were doing what the minister is doing now, introducing identical measures.
Oh, no.

So far as the measures are concerned, yes, but as to limitation on the amount to be spent, no. I will name the measures one after another. Farm placement has been in force since 1932, and before. It was introduced by the former government and carried into effect. Take the question of grants in aid to provinces; take the question

of public works; take the 1930 appropriation of $20,000,000; take assistance for direct relief-all this we were carrying out.
But under a blank cheque.

Certainly, because conditions in the country were such that we did not desire to place a limitation upon what we might be able to do. We will not go into that ground, but the fact is that the measures were the same as those to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North has just referred. When I recall the bitterness of the attacks and the personal abuse that took place of members of the government; when I recall what my colleagues had to meet, I think the minister is ill-advised when he states that there are members of this house who do not desire to see progress made in an ordered way. We will yield neither to him nor to anyone else in our desire to see this country get out of the difficulties it is now in. None of us will yield for a single moment to him in that desire, and when he suggests that there are members of this house who, because of political or other reasons, are not anxious to see his efforts succeed;-
When was that statement made, and where, if I may ask?
Just a few moments ago.
I am quite willing to leave it to my right hon. friend to read Hansard to-morrow.
It was made this evening.
I think he will find that no statement of that kind came from me.
The statement was that he was not so sure there were not those in the house who did not share that view.
That is not the statement just made by my right hon. friend.

I certainly do not want to misrepresent the hon. gentleman. I listened with great interest to what he was saying, as I always do, and I understood him to say that we were going forward in an ordered way; that if we did not go forward we could not make the progress we desired. As he said before, activity is not progress. He said he was not quite sure that there were not members of this house who did not share his view and who did not desire to see his efforts towards ordered progress succeed.
I am sure that is not the suggestion made by my right hon. friend a moment ago.

That is what I was endeavouring to say. I do not desire in any sense

to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, far from it. I heard the burst of applause which followed what was said by the minister because in the discussion of this item he was assuming an attitude of to some extent resenting criticism. I could not help thinking that these were
the same men.

not all of them, but the same
party-who sat here hour after hour and day after day, condemning the putting into effect, except as to the blank cheque, of the very same policies this committee is now asked to adopt. The minister suggests that there should be a sympathetic attitude

that is really the sense of his remarks-on the part of all members of this committee to men who are confronted for the first time with a new problem. Permit me to remind him that in August, 1930, the government was confronted with a new problem. Men who were inexperienced, who had not been prime minister of the country for eight or nine years, were faced with this problem. The statement is made as to cooperation not existing in this chamber, but I can remember a statement made just prior to the time the last Liberal budget was delivered; I can remember how the budget itself was framed and based upon the assumption that this country was going forward with continuous surpluses. The minister now suggests that we should take a reasonable and proper attitude towards the matter, and he is quite right. It was for that we pleaded; that was what we did not receive.
There was a change of government, and that change of government was predicated upon immediate action being taken to remedy what was represented as being an improper attitude of the then government towards this problem. Some of us have pointed out that you are following the same course as that of your predecessors, except that you have placed a limitation upon your bounty and upon your expenditures. It does not come with good grace when you complain that those who sit opposite point out that there has been no change except as to the extent to which you have limited your measures of relief. In other words, you have said to parliament, restrict and restrain, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has given the reason why. I am not going to discuss this. There were moments of great peril and great emergency in 1932 and we did not place a limitation upon anything except direct relief.
This government in its wisdom has placed a limitation upon the amounts that may be expended. Is that going to be a solution of the relief problem? Is that a measure of relief? Is that a new policy in connection with relief? Will that provide employment? Will that assist even one man to supply his

Speaker's Ruling
family with food and clothing? Will that give any of these men decent jobs? Will any of these things be done by placing a limitation upon it? I think not. I rose to-night merely to point out these matters and to direct attention to the continued criticism and almost merciless attacks which were made upon those charged with responsibility. We cannot be blamed for asking questions, for trying to obtain information as to the government's new policy. I agree with the minister when he says that he should not be blamed for profiting by the experience of the past. It is a matter of great gratification to us to realize that he has placed the imprimatur of his high approval upon our experience.

I would not for one moment seek to deprive the right hon. gentleman of any solace of vindication which he is able to discover in the policies we have adopted However I think it should be brought to the attention of the committee that when the previous opposition took exception to the policies followed by the right hon. gentleman and his followers, it was because of the unlimited powers which were not only given, but exercised in a large measure under the relief acts of that period. I hold in my hand a statement consisting of three pages outlining the various undertakings which were entered into under the blank cheque provisions of the relief legislation. I think my right hon. friend will recognize that in my whole handling of this unemployment question,, I have sought to avoid recriminations.
I agree with that.

I still intend to do so because it seems to me that the problem is too grave for partisan controversy. I should like also to correct any idea that I resent criticism. I do not resent criticism. As a matter of fact I think anyone entering the Department of Labour at the present time should expect criticism. He should be grateful for it when it is constructive. Even when it is not, he should realize that his reasoning is by no means infallible, and I can assure hon. members that the various suggestions which have been brought forward in these discussions will receive such consideration as we are able to give them. This problem is one which deserves the earnest attention, not only of this government but of this parliament.

And of the people of Canada.
